signal.title: fix(guardrails): record MCP tool guardrail evaluations and blocks in …
signal.text: > Base branch: `litellm_internal_staging` ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Guardrails Monitor reports 0 evaluations for all MCP tool traffic - It also reports 0 blocks, so MCP guardrails look inert - Admins cannot tell a firing MCP guardrail from a broken one How it solves it: - Threads the request's logger into the MCP guardrail hooks - Bridges guardrail decision records onto that logger - Flushes failure logging before the spend-log row is written - Covers every MCP tool entry point, Responses API included ## User Flow Before: a proxy admin who put a guardrail on MCP tool calls sees the Guardrails Monitor stay empty, so the guardrail looks dead even while it is refusing calls 1. They configure a guardrail on their MCP tool traffic and restart the proxy 2. They call an MCP tool through `POST http://localhost:4000/mcp` and it succeeds 3. They call it again with input the guardrail refuses, and the tool call comes back as an error naming the guardrail, so the guardrail is provably running 4. They open http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=guardrails and the monitor shows Total Evaluations 0 and Total Blocked 0 5. They open http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=logs, click into either MCP tool call, and the row carries no guardrail detail at all 6. Having no way to tell a working MCP guardrail from a misconfigured one, they cannot report on or alert off MCP guardrail activity After: the same steps, and the monitor now counts both the allowed evaluation and the refusal 1. They configure a guardrail on their MCP tool traffic and restart the proxy 2. They call an MCP tool through `POST http://localhost:4000/mcp` and it succeeds 3. They call it again with input the guardrail refuses, and the tool call comes back as an error naming the guardrail 4. They open http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=guardrails and the monitor shows Total Evaluations 2 and Total Blocked 1 5. They open http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=logs, click into either MCP tool call, and the row shows which guardrail ran and whether it allowed or blocked 6. They can now report on and alert off MCP guardrail activity the same way they already do for chat completions ## Relevant issues Reimplements #34249 (Eugene Yao) on current `litellm_internal_staging`, written from scratch against today's staging rather than rebased, since the MCP tool-call path moved underneath it It also lands the review feedback #34249 collected. This one is based on `litellm_internal_staging` instead of `main`. It reuses the `function_setup` call the Responses API MCP path already makes rather than adding a second one. It drops the metadata aliasing, so the synthetic guardrail request's metadata bucket is left as `_convert_mcp_to_llm_format` built it and nothing else reads through an alias. And it threads the Responses API entry point, which the original left on the old behavior, so `/v1/responses` MCP tool calls are counted too ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5677 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix End to end against a real proxy on `localhost:4000` backed by a real Postgres, driven by real MCP tool calls over streamable HTTP, with the counts read back from the same endpoint the Admin UI Guardrails Monitor page calls. No mocks anywhere in this section Before commit: `2bc9bb4a9d308fd8791e8af67d2e5bd92f6d5947` (this PR's parent) After commit: `c3576be27bb052e0fb49bd15863398a2b9547605` The branch has since been squashed to the current tip `9858d021eef07fefb955d7dc9d4c8e1595afb495`. Everything between the measured commit and that tip is comment and docstring wording, two rule-named `# noqa` suppressions, one return annotation, hoisting an import from function-local to module level, and one strengthened assertion in a test. Nothing that changes what the run above measured. All four legs were then re-run at that tip against the same parent commit on Python 3.12, this time through the plain `litellm --config` CLI path with no uvicorn workaround, and produced the identical table: before 0 and 0 with null `guardrail_information` in both configs, after 1 evaluated with 0 blocked for the allowing guardrail and 1 evaluated with 1 blocked for the blocking one, with `guardrail_information` present on the matching spend-log rows and `LiteLLM_DailyGuardrailMetrics` populated Setup is a synthetic MCP server exposing one tool, `synthetic_echo`, plus two probe guardrails registered on `mode: "pre_mcp_call"`, one that always allows and one that always blocks. Both subclass `CustomGuardrail` and carry `@log_guardrail_information`, so the real decorator path is exercised. The one configured model points at `http://127.0.0.1:9/unused` with a placeholder key, so no provider is ever contacted, and every tool argument is synthetic What the monitor actually reads: `GET /guardrails/usage/overview` in `litellm/proxy/guardrails/usage_endpoints.py`, which sums `LiteLLM_DailyGuardrailMetrics`. Those rows are aggregated by `process_spend_logs_guardrail_usage` out of `LiteLLM_SpendLogs.metadata->'guardrail_information'`. There is no dedicated guardrail column, so that one JSON key is the thing this PR makes appear | Tree | Guardrail | Tool call result | SpendLogs `status` | `metadata->'guardrail_information'` | `totalRequests` | `totalBlocked` | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Before | allow | `echo:synthetic-probe-003`, `isError:false` | `success` | **null** | **0** | **0** | | Before | block | `Error: Guardrail violation ... synthetic-block`, `isError:true` | `failure` | **null** | **0** | **0** | | After | allow | `echo:synthetic-probe-001`, `isError:false` | `success` | present, `guardrail_status: "success"` | **1** | **0** | | After | block | `Error: Guardrail violation ... synthetic-block`, `isError:true` | `failure` | present, `guardrail_status: "guardrail_intervened"` | **1** | **1** | `LiteLLM_DailyGuardrailMetrics` held zero rows on the before tree in both cases. On the after tree: ``` guardrail_id | date | requests_evaluated | passed_count | blocked_count ------------------+------------+--------------------+--------------+--------------- synthetic-allow | 2026-08-14 | 1 | 1 | 0 synthetic-block | 2026-08-14 | 1 | 0 | 1 ``` The blocked call's spend-log row on the after tree, read straight out of Postgres: ``` status | gi ---------+----------------------------------------------------- failure | [ + | { + | "duration": 0.000014, + | "end_time": 1786737260.155436, + | "start_time": 1786737260.155423, + | "guardrail_mode": "pre_call", + | "guardrail_name": "synthetic-block", + | "guardrail_status": "guardrail_intervened",+ | "guardrail_provider": null, + | "guardrail_response": "REDACTED_BY_LITELM",+ | "masked_entity_count": null + | } + | ] success | null (2 rows) ``` One thing worth stating precisely, because it bounds the claim: the before tree already wrote a `status="failure"` spend-log row for the blocked call. What changes here is that the row carries the guardrail decision record at all, and therefore that the monitor counts it. This PR does not create that failure row Scope of what the run above measures: `pre_mcp_call`, on the streamable HTTP `/mcp` route, for an authenticated key. The `during_mcp_call` hook and the Responses API entry point are covered by the unit tests rather than by this run, and blocks on anonymous calls are the known gap described under Caveats Reproducing it, with the proxy pointed at either tree by swapping `$TREE`, and the three tables truncated between runs so counts start at zero: ```bash export PATH="/path/to/venv/bin:$PATH" # the prisma CLI must be on PATH export DATABASE_URL='postgresql://postgres@127.0.0.1:55432/litellm' export TREE=/path/to/this/branch # or the parent commit's tree docker run -d --name mcpproof-pg -p 55432:5432 \ -e POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD=trust -e POSTGRES_DB=litellm postgres:16 prisma migrate deploy --schema="$TREE/litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/schema.prisma" python stub_mcp_server.py & # FastMCP, stateless_http, exposes synthetic_echo cd "$TREE" CONFIG_FILE_PATH=config_block.yaml python -m uvicorn litellm.proxy.proxy_server:app \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4000 --loop asyncio & until curl -sf localhost:4000/health/readiness >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done MCP=(-H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-1234' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' -H 'x-mcp-servers: synthetic_stub') curl -s http://localhost:4000/mcp/ "${MCP[@]}" -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"probe","version":"1"}}}' curl -s http://localhost:4000/mcp/ "${MCP[@]}" -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"synthetic_stub-synthetic_echo","arguments":{"text":"synthetic-probe-001"}}}' sleep 20 # spend-log flush plus daily-metrics aggregation curl -s "http://localhost:4000/guardrails/usage/overview?start_date=$(date +%F)&end_date=$(date +%F)" \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-1234' | python -m json.tool docker exec -i mcpproof-pg psql -U postgres -d litellm -c \ 'SELECT status, metadata->>'"'"'guardrail_information'"'"' FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs";' docker exec -i mcpproof-pg psql -U postgres -d litellm -c \ 'SELECT * FROM "LiteLLM_DailyGuardrailMetrics";' ``` Expected on the before tree: `totalRequests` 0, `totalBlocked` 0, `guardrail_information` null, `LiteLLM_DailyGuardrailMetrics` empty. On this branch: 1 and 1 for the blocking config, 1 and 0 for the allowing one. The equivalent in the UI is `http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=guardrails` going from an empty monitor to a populated one Two deviations from the standard local-proxy recipe, disclosed rather than papered over. First, `proxy_cli.py` hard-codes `uvloop` off Windows and uvloop does not import on Python 3.14 (`ImportError: cannot import name 'BaseDefaultEventLoopPolicy' from 'asyncio.events'`), so the identical ASGI app was launched through `uvicorn --loop asyncio` instead of `litellm --config ...`. Same `proxy_server:app`, same config loading, same routers, only the event loop and the CLI wrapper differ, and on Python 3.12 or older the normal command should work unchanged. Second, migrations had to be applied by hand with `prisma migrate deploy` because the proxy did not run them on startup. Both proxies also logged an unrelated `AttributeError: 'Batch' object has no attribute 'litellm_dailygatewayrequests'` from `gateway_request_tracking.py`, identically on both trees, which touches gateway request counts rather than guardrails and cannot bias the comparison ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Blocks on anonymous MCP calls are still not counted - That needs a counter outside SpendLogs, which is attributable - Only guardrail decision records are bridged onto the logger - Messages and tool arguments are deliberately not copied Anonymous MCP calls, spelled out because Greptile filed it as P1 twice on #34249 and it was declined there: a guardrail block on an unauthenticated MCP call still does not reach the monitor. The failure handlers now run for those calls, so OTel and the other failure sinks see the block, but `post_call_failure_hook` stays gated on an authenticated key. That gate is deliberate and predates this PR. The spend-log writer downstream of it dereferences authenticated key and budget data, and a SpendLogs row is an attributable billing and audit record, so an anonymous row has nothing to attribute. Counting anonymous blocks needs a counter that does not live in SpendLogs, which is a separate design change rather than something to bolt onto this fix. `test_block_flushes_failure_for_anonymous_calls` pins the current behavior so the gap is visible rather than silent On what gets recorded: only guardrail decision metadata moves onto the request logger, meaning the guardrail name, the event, the outcome and the timing. The synthetic guardrail request that MCP builds also holds the tool arguments and the LLM-shaped message list, and those are deliberately left behind. Nothing the monitor renders needs them, and copying them would push end-user payload into spend logs ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: [Bug]: GET /health returns extra_headers and aws_session_token in plaintext
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. Related, not a duplicate: #18818 fixed masking of `extra_headers` on `/model/info`. `GET /health` is a different sanitizer. It still returns those values in full. `api_key` is stripped (CVE-2025-11203 class). `extra_headers` and `aws_session_token` were never added to that strip list. ### What happened? LiteLLM 1.96.2. No master key. A deployment in `config.yaml` has `extra_headers` (Azure `api-key`, Google `x-goog-api-key`, a Bearer token) and `aws_session_token`. `GET /health` returns those values in plaintext on the healthy (or unhealthy) row. `api_key` is absent. `api_base` is absent for a non-admin caller. The extra headers stay. This was reproduced with fake `CANARY_*` strings, not real provider keys. A live proxy with a normal `api_key: os.environ/...` and no `extra_headers` does not echo the resolved key on `/model/info` (`api_key` is popped). The hole is specifically fields that are not `api_key`. Expected: `/health` should omit or mask `extra_headers`, `headers`, and `aws_session_token` the same way it already omits `api_key`. ### User Flow Before a (hypothetical) fix: a tenant who can call `/health` can read the admin's upstream credentials out of the JSON. 1. The proxy admin puts provider auth in `litellm_params.extra_headers` (and optionally `aws_session_token`) in `config.yaml`, then starts the proxy on `http://127.0.0.1:4000`. 2. Any caller sends `GET http://127.0.0.1:4000/health` with no `Authorization` header (default install, no master key). 3. HTTP 200. The `healthy_endpoints` (or `unhealthy_endpoints`) row contains `extra_headers.Authorization`, `extra_headers.x-goog-api-key`, `extra_headers.api-key`, and `aws_session_token` in full. 4. That caller can take those values and call the provider directly, bypassing the proxy. After a (hypothetical) fix: the same `/health` call still reports healthy/unhealthy, but those secret fields are gone or masked. 1. The proxy admin uses the same `config.yaml` and starts the same proxy. 2. The same caller sends `GET http://127.0.0.1:4000/health`. 3. HTTP 200. The row still has `model` and health status. It does not contain the `extra_headers` values or `aws_session_token`. 4. That caller cannot recover the admin's upstream credentials from `/health`. ### Proof the bug occurs Config / setup the proxy ran with: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: mock litellm_params: model: openai/mockmodel api_base: http://127.0.0.1:9996/v1 api_key: sk-x-CANARY_DEPLOYMENT_API_KEY extra_headers: Authorization: Bearer CANARY_EXTRA_HEADERS_AUTHORIZATION x-goog-api-key: CANARY_X_GOOG_API_KEY_VALUE api-key: CANARY_AZURE_STYLE_API_KEY aws_session_token: CANARY_AWS_SESSION_TOKEN_VALUE ``` The backend at `127.0.0.1:9996` is a local OpenAI-compatible stub that returns HTTP 200 so the row lands in `healthy_endpoints`. The leak is the proxy copying `litellm_params` into the `/health` body. It does not depend on a real provider key. You can drop the stub: point `api_base` at `http://127.0.0.1:1`. The health check fails, and the same fields still appear under `unhealthy_endpoints`. No API key required. Version or commit: LiteLLM **1.96.2** Commands and their full output: ``` curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4000/health ``` ```json { "healthy_endpoints": [ { "model": "openai/mockmodel", "extra_headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer CANARY_EXTRA_HEADERS_AUTHORIZATION", "x-goog-api-key": "CANARY_X_GOOG_API_KEY_VALUE", "api-key": "CANARY_AZURE_STYLE_API_KEY" }, "aws_session_token": "CANARY_AWS_SESSION_TOKEN_VALUE" } ], "unhealthy_endpoints": [], "healthy_count": 1, "unhealthy_count": 0 } ``` `api_key` is not in that object. `GET /v1/models` and `GET /health/liveliness` do not contain the canaries. Copy-paste repro, no keys, no stub: ```yaml # leak.yaml model_list: - model_name: demo litellm_params: model: openai/gpt-4o-mini api_base: http://127.0.0.1:1 api_key: sk-not-a-real-key extra_headers: x-goog-api-key: CANARY_X_GOOG_API_KEY_VALUE api-key: CANARY_AZURE_STYLE_API_KEY aws_session_token: CANARY_AWS_SESSION_TOKEN_VALUE ``` ``` litellm --config leak.yaml --port 4000 --host 127.0.0.1 curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4000/health ``` The canaries show up on the unhealthy row. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.96.2

signal.title: [Bug]: LiteLLM proxy silently returns understated token counts when Bedrock CountTokens is unsupported for a model
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? `bedrock-runtime`'s `CountTokens` API does not support most current Anthropic models — including **Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5** (full matrix below; of the current line-up only Sonnet 4.6 works). When it rejects a model, the proxy logs a warning and falls through to its local tokenizer. For these models the local tokenizer is badly miscalibrated, so `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` returns a **confidently wrong, much lower number** with a `200 OK` and no indication to the caller that the value is an estimate. Clients that use `count_tokens` for context management (Claude Code / Claude Desktop do) therefore believe they have far more headroom than they do, keep growing the conversation, and eventually get a hard `400 prompt is too long` from the provider — long after any context-compaction threshold should have fired. ### User Flow **Before a (hypothetical) fix: a developer running Claude Code against the proxy is told their conversation is ~675K tokens when the model actually measures it at ~1.19M, so their client never trims it and the next turn is rejected outright.** 1. They export `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://litellm-domain` and `ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-opus-5`, then start a long refactoring session in Claude Code. 2. As the conversation grows, their client sends `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages/count_tokens` with `{"model": "claude-opus-5", "messages": [...the whole conversation...]}`. 3. It comes back `200 OK` with `{"input_tokens": 675431}` — a plain number, with nothing marking it as an estimate rather than a figure the model itself confirmed. 4. Their client compares 675,431 against the 1,000,000-token window Opus 5 advertises, concludes it is at ~68% capacity, and does not summarise or trim anything. 5. They send the next turn: `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages` with `{"model": "claude-opus-5", "max_tokens": 4096, "messages": [...the same conversation...]}`. 6. It comes back **`400`** with `{"type":"error","error":{"type":"invalid_request_error", "message":"...prompt is too long: 1227544 tokens > 1000000 maximum"}}` — the model counted the identical conversation as **1,227,544** tokens, roughly 1.8× the number they were given in step 3. 7. Every retry fails the same way. Nothing they can request from the proxy reports a number anywhere near 1.2M, so from their seat the rejection has no visible cause. 8. If the proxy has `fallbacks` configured, they never see the 400 at all: the turn returns `200` and at `https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs` that request is listed against **`claude-sonnet-4-6`**, not the `claude-opus-5` they asked for — with the whole conversation re-charged as fresh input, so its cost on that page is roughly 9× the neighbouring turns. **After a (hypothetical) fix: the same call reports a count the model agrees with, so their client trims in time and the turn succeeds on the model they asked for.** 1. They export `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://litellm-domain` and `ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-opus-5`, then start a long refactoring session in Claude Code. 2. As the conversation grows, their client sends `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages/count_tokens` with `{"model": "claude-opus-5", "messages": [...the whole conversation...]}`. 3. It comes back `200 OK` with `{"input_tokens": 1227544}` — matching what the model itself counts. (Equally acceptable from the user's seat: a `4xx` saying the count is unavailable for this model, which at least tells their client not to trust a guess.) 4. Their client compares 1,227,544 against the 1,000,000-token window, sees it is over capacity, and summarises the earlier part of the conversation before sending anything. 5. They send the next turn: `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages` with `{"model": "claude-opus-5", "max_tokens": 4096, "messages": [...the trimmed conversation...]}`. 6. It comes back **`200 OK`** with `"model": "claude-opus-5"` and a normal `usage` block. 7. The session continues. Trimming happens whenever the reported count approaches the window, so the wall is never hit. 8. At `https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs` every turn is listed against `claude-opus-5`, at costs consistent with its neighbours. ### Proof the bug occurs ## Steps to reproduce 1. Configure any model whose Bedrock `CountTokens` support is absent — e.g. ```yaml model_list: - model_name: claude-opus-5 litellm_params: model: bedrock/global.anthropic.claude-opus-5 aws_region_name: us-east-1 ``` 2. `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` with `{"model": "claude-opus-5", "messages": [...]}` 3. Observe `200 OK` with an `input_tokens` value, and in the proxy log: ``` LiteLLM:ERROR: handler.py:123 - HTTP error in CountTokens handler: Client error '400 Bad Request' for url 'https://bedrock-runtime.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/model/anthropic.claude-opus-5/count-tokens' LiteLLM:WARNING: bedrock_token_counter.py:91 - Bedrock CountTokens API error: status=400, message={"message":"The provided model doesn't support counting tokens."} LiteLLM Proxy:WARNING: proxy_server.py:8772 - Provider token counting failed (400): {"message":"The provided model doesn't support counting tokens."}. Falling back to local tokenizer. ``` ## Scope: this affects every current-generation Claude model on Bedrock This is not one edge-case model. Probed directly against `bedrock-runtime` in `us-east-1` (`aws bedrock-runtime count-tokens --model-id <id> --input '{"invokeModel":{"body":"…"}}'`, body containing a valid Anthropic Messages payload with `max_tokens`): | Model ID | Bedrock `CountTokens` | |---|---| | `anthropic.claude-opus-5` | ❌ `ValidationException: The provided model doesn't support counting tokens.` | | `anthropic.claude-opus-4-8` | ❌ same | | `anthropic.claude-sonnet-5` | ❌ same | | `us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0` | ❌ same | | `anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5` | ❌ `The provided model identifier is invalid.` | | **`anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6`** | ✅ **works** — returns `{"inputTokens": 26}` | | `global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6` | ❌ unsupported — **the geo prefix alone breaks a model that works bare** | So of the current Claude line-up, **only Sonnet 4.6 can be counted on `bedrock-runtime`.** Every other model — including Opus 5 and Sonnet 5, the current defaults — takes the local-tokenizer path on every `count_tokens` call. Two diagnostic notes for whoever picks this up: - A **different** error message (`max_tokens: Field required`) means the model *is* supported and only the request body was wrong. `"doesn't support counting tokens"` is the real rejection, and is what should gate any retry logic. - The proxy already strips the geo/global prefix when building the CountTokens URL (the logged URL is `/model/anthropic.claude-opus-5/count-tokens` for a model configured as `bedrock/global.anthropic.claude-opus-5`), which is correct — passing the prefixed ID through would fail even for Sonnet 4.6. Worth preserving if this code is touched. ## Measured error Identical text throughout. `claude-sonnet-4-6` *is* supported by Bedrock CountTokens, so it gives an authoritative reference count; the target model's true count comes from the provider's own rejection message, which states both the count and the limit. **Tokenizer ratio** — same text, two models: | source | tokens | |---|---| | `anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6` via Bedrock `CountTokens` (authoritative) | 745,753 | | `global.anthropic.claude-opus-5` — from `ValidationException: prompt is too long: 1227544 tokens > 1000000 maximum` | **1,227,544** | | ratio | **1.646×** | **What the proxy reports** — same 400-paragraph sample: | source | tokens | |---|---| | Bedrock `CountTokens` for `claude-sonnet-4-6` (authoritative) | 12,025 | | proxy `count_tokens` for `claude-sonnet-4-6` | 12,025 ✅ exact (provider path used) | | proxy `count_tokens` for `claude-opus-5` | **11,208** ⬅ local tokenizer, 0.93× the sonnet count | | `claude-opus-5` real count (0.93 → 1.646 correction) | **~19,793** | **The proxy understates this model by ~1.77×.** Note the local tokenizer returns *slightly fewer* tokens than the older model's tokenizer, while the target model's real tokenizer produces considerably more — the two errors compound. ## Impact With a 1,000,000-token model limit, the effective ceiling expressed in numbers the proxy reports is about **565K**. A client that compacts at, say, 80% of the advertised window would trigger at 800K reported — i.e. **~1.41M real, which is past the hard limit.** The safety mechanism is unreachable: the request fails before the threshold is ever approached. Observed in production: a long agentic session ran to ~1.19–1.22M real tokens while the client believed it was around 675K, then failed with `prompt is too long`. Requests below the boundary succeeded normally, so the failure is purely a function of size. Two secondary effects worth noting: 1. **Cost.** If `litellm_settings.fallbacks` is configured, the resulting 400 is silently retried on the fallback model. Prompt caches are per-model, so the fallback runs cold and re-reads the entire context at full price. In our case the per-request cost rose roughly 9×, with no error surfaced to the client and — see below — nothing in the logs. 2. **CPU.** Local tokenization of very large contexts is expensive. Repeated `count_tokens` calls over ~150K-token conversations saturated one of two vCPUs on the proxy host, causing an outage: the app stayed internally healthy while throughput collapsed and health checks timed out. ## Reproduction helper Deliberately overshooting is free — a rejected request is not billed, and the error names both the real token count and the limit, which is the only way we found to obtain a ground-truth count for a model Bedrock will not count: ```python import json, boto3 br = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1") br.invoke_model(modelId="global.anthropic.claude-opus-5", body=json.dumps({ "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31", "max_tokens": 16, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "<oversized text>"}]})) # botocore.errorfactory.ValidationException: # prompt is too long: 1227544 tokens > 1000000 maximum ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? 1.96.2 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Codex sends `client_metadata`, Bedrock Converse rejects the call - `drop_params` never removed it, so the route was unusable - Anthropic and Vertex were already fixed in #29489 How it solves it: - Drop `client_metadata` from `additionalModelRequestFields` in Converse - Regression test asserts real passthrough fields still survive ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5232 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Codex is the only client that sends `client_metadata`, so the failure only shows up on Codex -> proxy -> Bedrock. Converse forwards anything it doesn't recognize as `additionalModelRequestFields`, Bedrock hands that to the model verbatim, and Anthropic answers with `client_metadata: Extra inputs are not permitted` Proxy config used for both runs: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: claude-opus-4-8 litellm_params: model: bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-opus-4-8 aws_region_name: us-west-2 litellm_settings: drop_params: true ``` Same curl for both runs, the exact body Codex sends: ```bash curl -s -X POST http://localhost:4000/v1/responses \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-1234' \ -d '{"model":"claude-opus-4-8","input":"say hi","max_output_tokens":16,"client_metadata":{"originator":"codex_cli_rs"}}' ``` Before, at 0659738b3e, the request the proxy builds for Bedrock (from `--detailed_debug`, `drop_params: true` active and not helping): ``` -d '{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "say hi"}]}], "inferenceConfig": {"maxTokens": 16}, "additionalModelRequestFields": {"client_metadata": {"originator": "codex_cli_rs"}}}' ``` After, at cdac5fde0e, same curl, no passthrough field left for Bedrock to reject: ``` -d '{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "say hi"}]}], "inferenceConfig": {"maxTokens": 16}}' ``` Both runs stopped at Bedrock auth: the AWS credentials I have access to are no longer authorized for `bedrock:InvokeModel` on this account, so I could not get a paid 200 back. The before/after difference is in the request LiteLLM signs and sends, which is exactly the field Bedrock was rejecting, so someone with working Bedrock credentials can confirm the 200 in a minute Until a release ships, `additional_drop_params: ["client_metadata"]` on the model works as a config-only workaround, and it stays a valid escape hatch afterwards ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Changes `AmazonConverseConfig._prepare_request_params` drops `client_metadata` next to where it already drops `parallel_tool_calls`, so it never reaches `additionalModelRequestFields`. `AnthropicConfig.transform_request` does the same thing for the direct Anthropic, Vertex, and Bedrock invoke paths, this closes the one remaining hole Note that `drop_params` is the wrong lever here and always was: it only governs known OpenAI params a provider does not support, while `client_metadata` is not an OpenAI param, so it flows through the provider-specific passthrough instead ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/e57cd0ce775749e595f7da41d0795378

signal.title: feat(otel/v2)!: admin-owned, identity-scoped trace destinations
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - OTEL traces could only go to one proxy-wide destination set configured in `config.yaml`, so there was no way to route different teams' traces to different backends - in a shared observability tool, one tenant could see another tenant's traces How it solves it: - admins register trace destinations as credentials with an identity-scoped access grant, and each request fans its trace out to exactly the destinations its team or org is granted - default-deny throughout, with `LITELLM_OTEL_V2` as the sole activation gate ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-3850 ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Changes Reviewed as five stacked PRs: the credential model and destination mapping (#35513), request-time resolution (#35514), export and fan-out (#35515), disclosure on the team and org info pages (#35516), and the admin UI (#35517). The design principle worth stating explicitly is that a destination is a sink and never a reason to change ownership. Which logger owns a backend is decided by the operator's own configuration; admin destinations are delivered to separately, by a process-wide destination logger. An earlier revision of this stack coupled the two, and registering a destination scoped to one team moved every other tenant onto a different logger for the life of the process, costing them their prompt content. That coupling is gone. Correcting a claim that appeared in an earlier revision of this description: v2 does not own a backend only when an admin destination exists for it. The flag plus the operator's credentials decide ownership, and a destination does not change that answer. ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Live proxy throughout, real Bedrock, real Langfuse and real Arize readback, no mocks. Per-layer evidence is in each stacked PR. Tenant isolation on one proxy: ``` team A granted a destination receives its full trace there team B granted nothing receives nothing there, keeps its own pipeline unchanged client-supplied otel_destinations ignored, zero spans at the attacker target ``` ## QA runbook See the QA runbook in each stacked PR; they are meant to be exercised in order. ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: fix(proxy): registry caches stop per-request tag and end-user Postgres reads in auth
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Every tagged request queries Postgres for tags that have no row - Every request carrying a user id queries Postgres for that end user - Under connection pool contention these per-request reads queue for minutes inside auth How it solves it: - Cache the bounded set of registered tag names under one key - Cache the bounded set of restricted end user ids the same way - Requests with unregistered tags and unrestricted users now do zero DB reads - Tag and customer endpoints evict both caches and broadcast cross-worker invalidation ## User Flow Before: a high-volume classification service stalls and times out every night right after 00:00 UTC 1. The service sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with a virtual key, `"user": "<their-customer-id>"`, and `"metadata": {"tags": ["llm_classification"]}` on every request 2. Responses normally come back in well under a second, and the usage dashboard attributes spend per tag and per customer 3. Right after 00:00 UTC the same request averages 11s with a p95 of 80s, blowing past the caller's 15s deadline, so their jobs fail and retry 4. Retries pile up, the gateway pods fail health checks and restart, the load balancer returns 503s, and on-call gets paged After: the same nightly window passes without the service noticing 1. The service sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with a virtual key, `"user": "<their-customer-id>"`, and `"metadata": {"tags": ["llm_classification"]}` on every request 2. Responses normally come back in well under a second, and the usage dashboard attributes spend per tag and per customer 3. Right after 00:00 UTC the same request still comes back in well under a second 4. No timeouts, no retry storm, no restarts, no pages ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Refs LIT-5438 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [ ] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Live proxy, real Groq calls costing real money, no mocks. Both proxies ran against the same Postgres with a config whose only relevant settings are one Groq model plus `disable_spend_updates: true` and `disable_spend_logs: true`, which turn off the async spend writer so that every scan counted below is an auth-path read. Scans measured with ```sql SELECT COALESCE(SUM(seq_scan+idx_scan) FILTER (WHERE relname='LiteLLM_TagTable'),0), COALESCE(SUM(seq_scan+idx_scan) FILTER (WHERE relname='LiteLLM_EndUserTable'),0) FROM pg_stat_user_tables; ``` sampled before and after each request, with a 5s idle-drift sample first proving ambient noise was zero. Each run generates a fresh virtual key, then sends identical requests with a free-form tag and a distinct `user` per request ```bash curl -s http://localhost:$PORT/key/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-1234' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"key_alias":"lit5438-proof"}' curl -s http://localhost:$PORT/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $VIRTUAL_KEY" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"groq-qwen3-6","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"ping"}], "user":"lit5438-user-N","metadata":{"tags":["lit5438-tag"]}}' ``` Before, at the merge base 09889e1986: ``` idle drift over 5s (ambient noise): tag-table 0 end-user-table 0 request 1: HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 2 end-user-table scans: 2 request 2: HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 0 end-user-table scans: 1 request 3: HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 4 end-user-table scans: 3 TOTAL over 3 requests: tag-table 6 end-user-table 6 warm-path request 4 (writer settled): HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 2 end-user-table scans: 2 warm-path request 5 (writer settled): HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 2 end-user-table scans: 2 ``` After, at c13c442446: ``` idle drift over 5s (ambient noise): tag-table 0 end-user-table 0 request 1: HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 0 end-user-table scans: 0 request 2: HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 1 end-user-table scans: 1 request 3: HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 0 end-user-table scans: 0 TOTAL over 3 requests: tag-table 1 end-user-table 1 warm-path request 4 (writer settled): HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 0 end-user-table scans: 0 warm-path request 5 (writer settled): HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 0 end-user-table scans: 0 ``` Before pays 2 scans per table on every request forever. After pays exactly one registry load per table, then zero, including for user ids the proxy has never seen. Postgres stats flush lag of a few seconds shifts some counts one row down, which is why the one-time registry load shows on the request 2 row Same measurement on the other two LLM endpoints, sent with `litellm_metadata.tags` and a fresh user id each. Before at 09889e1986: ``` /v1/messages: HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 2 end-user-table scans: 2 /v1/responses: HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 2 end-user-table scans: 2 ``` After at c13c442446, where /v1/messages lands one registry reload because the 60s TTL had lapsed between runs, and /v1/responses rides it: ``` /v1/messages: HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 1 end-user-table scans: 1 /v1/responses: HTTP 200 tag-table scans: 0 end-user-table scans: 0 ``` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Tag rows written outside the API enforce within one 60s TTL per pod - Without coordination Redis, other workers converge within the same TTL - Default end user budgets or DB id validation bypass the skip entirely - Pre-existing, tracked separately: /customer/update silently drops `blocked: false` - Pre-existing, tracked separately: deletes leave spend counters behind ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: feat(vector_stores): add Valkey as a managed vector store provider
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - No vector store provider for Valkey / valkey-search - Managed vector store pipeline assumed every provider speaks HTTP How it solves it: - New valkey provider embeds the query and runs a KNN FT.SEARCH - BaseDirectVectorStoreConfig lets RESP datastores bypass the HTTP pipeline - Admin UI Add Vector Store modal gains a Valkey provider, with a plain-English setup checklist, explicit per-field tooltips, and the embedding model picked from the proxy's models like Milvus and S3 Vectors - Also registrable via vector_store_registry in the proxy config - Bounded socket timeouts so unreachable hosts cannot pin workers ## User Flow Before: a proxy admin whose document embeddings already live in Valkey cannot search them through the gateway 1. They open http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=vector-stores and click Add Vector Store: the provider dropdown offers Bedrock, S3 Vectors, pgvector, Vertex AI, OpenAI, Azure, and Milvus, but no Valkey 2. There is no provider value they can pass to POST http://localhost:4000/vector_store/new that would make POST http://localhost:4000/v1/vector_stores/{id}/search read from their Valkey index, so their documents stay unreachable After: the same admin registers the Valkey index and searches it from the API, the UI, and the config 1. They open http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=vector-stores and click Add Vector Store: the dropdown now shows Valkey with its logo, and selecting it reveals host, port, password, TLS, embedding model, text field, and vector field inputs plus a setup checklist spelling out that LiteLLM only searches an index they already built, that vector search must be enabled on the server, and that the embedding model and field names must match what they stored 2. They enter their Valkey host and port, the FT index name as the Vector Store ID, and pick the embedding model from the proxy's models, click Create, and see the store listed with provider Valkey 3. On the Test Vector Store tab they type a question and get their own documents back ranked by score 4. The same store answers POST http://localhost:4000/v1/vector_stores/{id}/search with an OpenAI-shaped results page, and an identical entry declared under vector_store_registry in the proxy config works without touching the UI or the management API ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-4842 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [ ] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix All proofs captured at 10a95d0dd3 against a live proxy on localhost:4842, with real Vertex AI embedding calls (vertex_ai/gemini-embedding-001) costing real money. The datastore is a valkey/valkey-bundle container (valkey-search module loaded) on localhost:6390, holding an FT index named litellm-qa-docs over 6 HASH docs whose embedding field was seeded with the same model API path: create the store, search it twice, delete it ``` $ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:4842/vector_store/new -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"vector_store_id": "litellm-qa-docs", "custom_llm_provider": "valkey", "vector_store_name": "Valkey QA Docs", "litellm_params": {"valkey_host": "localhost", "valkey_port": 6390, "litellm_embedding_model": "vertex_ai/gemini-embedding-001"}}' {"status":"success","message":"Vector store litellm-qa-docs created successfully","vector_store":{"vector_store_id":"litellm-qa-docs","custom_llm_provider":"valkey","vector_store_name":"Valkey QA Docs",...,"litellm_params":{"valkey_host":"localhost","valkey_port":6390,...,"litellm_embedding_model":"vertex_ai/gemini-embedding-001",...},"team_id":null,"user_id":"default_user_id"}} $ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:4842/v1/vector_stores/litellm-qa-docs/search -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"query": "how do I pull a great espresso shot?", "max_num_results": 3}' {"object":"vector_store.search_results.page","search_query":"how do I pull a great espresso shot?","data":[{"score":0.787654995918,"content":[{"text":"To brew great espresso, use freshly roasted beans ground fine, 18 grams in, 36 grams out in about 28 seconds at 93 degrees Celsius.","type":"text"}],"file_id":"kb:espresso","filename":"kb:espresso"},{"score":0.53844845295,"content":[{"text":"Laminated croissant dough requires folding cold butter into the detrempe over several turns to build flaky layers.","type":"text"}],"file_id":"kb:croissant","filename":"kb:croissant"},{"score":0.451147139072,"content":[{"text":"Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun; Open http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=vector-stores and go to Manage Vector Stores, then click + Add Vector Store 2. Pick Valkey in the provider dropdown (renders with the Valkey logo) and note the setup alert plus the seven provider fields appearing 3. Fill Vector Store ID with the FT index name, Valkey Host, Valkey Port, and Embedding Model, then click Create and see the success toast and the new row with provider Valkey 4. Open the Test Vector Store tab, select the store, submit a query like "how do I make croissants flaky?", and see the matching doc as Result 1 with the highest score Add New Vector Store modal with Valkey selected: ![Add New Vector Store modal with the Valkey provider, setup alert, and connection fields](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/litellm_lit_4842_screenshots/valkey_ui_add_modal.png) Manage Vector Stores after creation: ![Manage Vector Stores table listing the store with provider Valkey](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/litellm_lit_4842_screenshots/valkey_ui_manage_row.png) Test Vector Store tab returning the seeded docs ranked by score: ![Test Vector Store tab showing six ranked results with the croissant doc first](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/litellm_lit_4842_screenshots/valkey_ui_test_results.png) ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats (if any) - Search only: file ingestion is not supported, valkey is excluded from the RAG upload dropdown - Docs page is written but must land in the separate docs repo - provider_endpoints_support.json docs link 404s until that docs page lands - Requires the valkey-search module and a pre-created FT index over HASH docs ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: [Bug]: CheckBatchCost stale sweep excludes completed statuses that its own job selection includes, so a completed unprocessed row is never swept and is polled indefinitely
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [X] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? A managed batch row with `status='completed'` and `batch_processed=false` is not marked `stale_expired` by `_cleanup_stale_managed_objects` regardless of age, while the poller's own job-selection query continues to return it on every cycle. Observed on two rows seeded 30 days old (`MANAGED_OBJECT_STALENESS_CUTOFF_DAYS=7`), identical except for `status`: | row | status before | status after sweep | batch_processed | still selected by poller | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `u02-inprogress` | `in_progress` | `stale_expired` | false | no | | `u02-completed` | `completed` | `completed` | false | yes | The sweep reported `marked 1 stale managed objects`, not 2. ### Code as it stands at v1.94.3 `enterprise/litellm_enterprise/proxy/common_utils/check_batch_cost.py:64`, the sweep: ```python async def _cleanup_stale_managed_objects(self) -> None: """ Mark managed objects older than MANAGED_OBJECT_STALENESS_CUTOFF_DAYS days in non-terminal states as 'stale_expired'. These will never complete and should not be polled. """ cutoff = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=MANAGED_OBJECT_STALENESS_CUTOFF_DAYS) result = await self.prisma_client.db.litellm_managedobjecttable.update_many( where={ "file_purpose": "batch", "status": {"not_in": ["completed", "complete", "failed", "expired", "cancelled", "stale_expired"]}, "created_at": {"lt": cutoff}, }, data={"status": "stale_expired"}, ) ``` `:527`, the job selection in the same class, run immediately after the sweep in `check_batch_cost()`: ```python if self._has_batch_processed_column: try: # Include "complete"/"completed" batches: the retrieve_batch # endpoint may transition a batch to "complete" before # CheckBatchCost runs. The batch_processed=False filter # already prevents reprocessing finished batches. jobs = await self.prisma_client.db.litellm_managedobjecttable.find_many( where={ "file_purpose": "batch", "batch_processed": False, "status": { "not_in": [ "failed", "expired", "cancelled", "stale_expired", ] }, }, take=MAX_OBJECTS_PER_POLL_CYCLE, order={"created_at": "asc"}, ) ``` The sweep's `not_in` list contains `completed` and `complete`; the selection's `not_in` list does not. --- ### User Flow **Before a (hypothetical) fix: an operator reviewing the batch backlog finds rows that neither clear nor age out** 1. They open `https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs` and see batch activity recorded normally for recent jobs 2. Reviewing older batch records, they find entries that reached a completed state weeks ago but are still listed as awaiting cost reconciliation 3. They wait past the documented staleness window and check again; the same entries are still listed as awaiting reconciliation, unchanged 4. Entries in a non-completed state from the same period are no longer listed, having been aged out 5. The entries remain in that state indefinitely, and each occupies one of the fixed number of slots the background reconciliation reads per cycle, so newer batches queue behind them 6. No API call fails and nothing is logged as an error at any point **After a (hypothetical) fix: the same rows either reconcile or age out, and the backlog drains** 1. They open `https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs` and see batch activity recorded normally for recent jobs 2. Reviewing older batch records, they find entries that reached a completed state weeks ago but are still listed as awaiting cost reconciliation 3. They wait past the documented staleness window and check again; those entries have left the awaiting state 4. Entries in a non-completed state from the same period have also aged out 5. No entry occupies a reconciliation slot indefinitely, so newer batches are read on the following cycle 6. No API call fails and nothing is logged as an error at any point --- ### Proof the bug occurs **Version**: `litellm 1.94.3`, image digest `sha256:b7d979bac2a9e8fbb7d55272ef5f1f4a08ab365de8f78b1800834ca718d4c941`. Constants in effect on the running proxy: `MANAGED_OBJECT_STALENESS_CUTOFF_DAYS = 7`, `MAX_OBJECTS_PER_POLL_CYCLE = 50`. This path is entirely internal to the proxy and its database; no provider call is involved in the sweep. **Config the proxy ran with** ```yaml model_list: - model_name: gpt-5-batch litellm_params: model: azure/gpt-5-batch-2025-08-07 api_base: os.environ/AZURE_API_BASE api_key: os.environ/AZURE_API_KEY general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL ``` Proxy started with `PROXY_BATCH_POLLING_INTERVAL=10` so cycles are observable. **Commands and their full output** Seed two rows 30 days old, both unprocessed, differing only in `status`: ``` $ psql -U llmproxy -d litellm -c " INSERT INTO \"LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable\" (id, unified_object_id, model_object_id, file_object, file_purpose, created_at, updated_at, status, batch_processed, created_by) VALUES ('u02-completed', 'u02-uoid-completed', 'u02-moid-completed', '{}'::jsonb, 'batch', NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days', NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days', 'completed', false, 'u02-test'), ('u02-inprogress', 'u02-uoid-inprogress', 'u02-moid-inprogress', '{}'::jsonb, 'batch', NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days', NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days', 'in_progress', false, 'u02-test'); SELECT id, status, batch_processed FROM \"LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable\" WHERE created_by='u02-test' ORDER BY id;" INSERT 0 2 id | status | batch_processed ----------------+-------------+----------------- u02-completed | completed | f u02-inprogress | in_progress | f (2 rows) ``` Wait one poll cycle and read the sweep's own log line: ``` $ docker logs --since 60s <proxy> 2>&1 | grep -o "CheckBatchCost: marked .* as stale_expired" CheckBatchCost: marked 1 stale managed objects (older than 7 days) as stale_expired ``` Row state after the sweep: ``` $ psql -U llmproxy -d litellm -c \ "SELECT id, status, batch_processed FROM \"LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable\" WHERE created_by='u02-test' ORDER BY id;" id | status | batch_processed ----------------+---------------+----------------- u02-completed | completed | f u02-inprogress | stale_expired | f (2 rows) ``` The two `where` clauses from the source above, run against the same rows. Sweep clause (`:71-76`): ``` $ psql -U llmproxy -d litellm -c " SELECT id, status FROM \"LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable\" WHERE file_purpose='batch' AND status NOT IN ('completed','complete','failed','expired','cancelled','stale_expired') AND created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days' AND created_by='u02-test';" id | status ----+-------- (0 rows) ``` Job-selection clause (`:533-546`): ``` $ psql -U llmproxy -d litellm -c " SELECT id, status FROM \"LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable\" WHERE file_purpose='batch' AND batch_processed = false AND status NOT IN ('failed','expired','cancelled','stale_expired') AND created_by='u02-test' ORDER BY created_at ASC;" id | status ---------------+----------- u02-completed | completed (1 row) ``` The `completed` row is matched by the selection clause and not by the sweep clause. The `in_progress` control row, seeded at the same age in the same statement, was swept. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.94.3

signal.title: test(e2e): replay a real tool-search assistant turn back to Bedrock Invoke
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - tool_search coverage stopped after the first turn - No test ever replayed a `server_tool_use` block back - A beta-header gap reached a customer unseen How it solves it: - Second probe replays the real assistant turn as history - Refuses to pass unless both server-tool blocks replayed - Harness tests cover the assertion's red paths - Test-only, no production code ## User Flow Before: a developer running Claude Code against a Bedrock Invoke deployment gets one good turn and then a 400 on the next, and nothing in our suite would have caught it 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages with a `tool_search_tool_regex_20251119` tool and get 200 back, carrying a `server_tool_use` block and the `tool_search_tool_result` answering it 2. They keep the conversation going, so the next POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages repeats those two blocks in `messages` with the same tools declared 3. If the gateway or the upstream mishandles those blocks, the turn fails and the session is dead from turn two onward, with a green compatibility matrix saying tool search works After: the same second turn is exercised on every matrix run, so the failure surfaces in CI instead of in a session 1. The matrix sends the same first POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages and takes the real answer back 2. It sends a second POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages carrying that answer verbatim in `messages`, with the tools still declared, answering any pending tool call with the id the model actually returned 3. A non-200 on that second turn turns the tool_search x Bedrock Invoke cell red and names which turn broke 4. A first turn that never produced the two blocks also turns the cell red rather than passing on an empty history ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5326 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Captured at `38eefb8c36`. No AWS credentials are available in this environment, so the Bedrock two-turn 200 is not run here; what follows is the request the probe puts on the wire, driven through the real Bedrock Invoke transform, plus a live confirmation of the same history against Anthropic direct The first turn is a real 200 from `api.anthropic.com` on `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` with `anthropic-beta: advanced-tool-use-2025-11-20`, and its answer is fed through the shipped helper to build turn 2 ``` turn 1 -> 200 turn 1 stop_reason: end_turn turn 1 block types: ['text', 'server_tool_use', 'tool_search_tool_result', 'text'] replayed server-tool block types: ['server_tool_use', 'tool_search_tool_result'] turn 2 (replayed history) -> 200 { "model": "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "done"}], "stop_reason": "end_turn", "usage": {"input_tokens": 1257, "output_tokens": 4} } ``` Both bodies then go through the real `AmazonAnthropicClaudeMessagesConfig.transform_anthropic_messages_request` for `us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0`, printing what Bedrock Invoke would receive. Turn 1 is what the existing probe already sends ```json { "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "If you have a tool to discover other tools, use it to find one. Otherwise reply with the word 'done'."} ], "max_tokens": 1024, "tools": [ {"type": "tool_search_tool_regex_20251119", "name": "tool_search_tool_regex"}, {"name": "add_numbers", "description": "Add two integers", "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"a": {"type": "integer"}, "b": {"type": "integer"}}, "required": ["a", "b"]}} ], "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31", "anthropic_beta": ["tool-search-tool-2025-10-19"] } -- anthropic_version injected (positive control): True -- server_tool_use: False -- tool_search_tool_result: False -- tool_search_tool_regex_20251119: True ``` Turn 2 is the new one, and this is the whole point of the PR: the history really does carry `server_tool_use` and `tool_search_tool_result` with the real `srvtoolu_` id ```json { "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "If you have a tool to discover other tools, use it to find one. Otherwise reply with the word 'done'."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": "I have a tool to discover other tools! Let me use it to search for available tools."}, {"type": "server_tool_use", "id": "srvtoolu_01Bq6v3jWFBhPuWokbvpg4iM", "name": "tool_search_tool_regex", "input": {"pattern": ".*"}}, {"type": "tool_search_tool_result", "tool_use_id": "srvtoolu_01Bq6v3jWFBhPuWokbvpg4iM", "content": {"type": "tool_search_tool_search_result", "tool_references": [{"type": "tool_reference", "tool_name": "tool_search_tool_regex"}, {"type": "tool_reference", "tool_name": "add_numbers"}]}}, {"type": "text", "text": "Great! I found the available tools: ..."} ]}, {"role": "user", "content": "Thanks. Now reply with the word 'done'."} ], "max_tokens": 64, "tools": [ {"type": "tool_search_tool_regex_20251119", "name": "tool_search_tool_regex"}, {"name": "add_numbers", "description": "Add two integers", "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"a": {"type": "integer"}, "b": {"type": "integer"}}, "required": ["a", "b"]}} ], "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31", "anthropic_beta": ["tool-search-tool-2025-10-19"] } -- anthropic_version injected (positive control): True -- server_tool_use: True -- tool_search_tool_result: True -- tool_search_tool_regex_20251119: True ``` Negative control, a plain user message with no tools through the same transform, showing none of the blocks appear and that the True's above are not printed unconditionally ```json { "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hello world"}], "max_tokens": 1024, "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31", "anthropic_beta": ["tool-search-tool-2025-10-19"] } -- anthropic_version injected (positive control): True -- server_tool_use: False -- tool_search_tool_result: False -- tool_search_tool_regex_20251119: False ``` The assertion's red paths never run in a green cell, so they get markerless harness tests. Mutating the missing-block check to `frozenset()` fails two of them, and the same run caught a real `NameError` in the rejection branch before this was pushed ``` tests/e2e/claude_code/_probe_unit_tests/test_http_probe.py ....... 7 passed in 0.01s ``` Both live tests collect, and the new cell is a known registry id (`python -m coverage_registry.collector --strict` exits 0 and does not list it as uncovered) ``` claude_code/tool_search/test_bedrock_invoke.py::test_tool_search_bedrock_invoke claude_code/tool_search/test_bedrock_invoke.py::test_tool_search_history_bedrock_invoke 2 tests collected in 0.02s ``` ## Type ✅ Test ## Caveats (if any) - Not run against Bedrock here: no AWS credentials - Anthropic direct accepts the replayed history, 200 - No CI job runs `tests/e2e/claude_code`; the matrix is driven manually - First turn needs 1024 max_tokens; 64 truncates the pair ## QA runbook - tests/e2e/claude_code/tool_search/test_bedrock_invoke.py::test_tool_search_history_bedrock_invoke - a real `server_tool_use` plus `tool_search_tool_result` pair, replayed as history with the tools still declared, is accepted by Bedrock Invoke on all three Claude tiers - [ ] Needs AWS credentials for Bedrock and a proxy fronting the `claude-haiku-4-5-bedrock-invoke`, `claude-sonnet-4-5-bedrock-invoke` and `claude-opus-4-7-bedrock-invoke` deployments, with `LITELLM_PROXY_URL` and `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` exported - [ ] POST /v1/messages with `max_tokens: 1024`, a `tool_search_tool_regex_20251119` tool plus one ordinary tool, and a prompt telling the model to discover its tools; expect 200 whose `content` holds a `server_tool_use` block and the `tool_search_tool_result` answering it - [ ] POST /v1/messages again with the same tools and three messages: the original user prompt, that assistant `content` array verbatim, and a follow-up user turn; expect 200 - [ ] Repeat both steps for the other two tiers - [ ] Sanity check: this test makes sense to add and is not hand-wavey (e.g., assert actual expected spend instead of just spend > 0) or potentially flaky ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > <sup>[Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) is generating a summary for commit 38eefb8c361b96627d2c5fa1843929e85b1d7156. signal.title: [Bug]: GET /v1/batches with after= does not advance: 99 batches walked in pages of 10 returned 16 distinct rows and has_more stayed true
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [X] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? On an account holding 99 managed batches, walking `GET /v1/batches?limit=10` and passing the `id` of each page's last item as `after` on the next request: - 15 pages returned 10 rows each, 150 rows total - 16 of those rows were distinct - 83 of the 99 batches did not appear in any page - `has_more` was `true` on every page, including page 15 Two consecutive pages at `limit=3` shared 2 of 3 rows. ### Code as it stands at v1.94.3 `litellm_enterprise/proxy/hooks/managed_files.py:318`: ```python if after: where_clause["id"] = {"gt": after} fetch_limit = limit or 20 if target_model_names: # Oversample so post-fetch model-name filtering still has enough rows. fetch_limit = max(fetch_limit * 3, 100) batches = await self.prisma_client.db.litellm_managedobjecttable.find_many( where=where_clause, take=fetch_limit, order={"created_at": "desc"}, ) ``` `:341`, inside the loop over `batches`: ```python batch_obj = LiteLLMBatch(**batch_data) batch_obj.id = batch.unified_object_id batch_objects.append(batch_obj) ``` `:354`: ```python return build_list_page( batch_objects, has_more=len(batch_objects) == (limit or 20) ) ``` `batch_objects` excludes rows dropped earlier in the same loop when `file_object` fails to parse, and rows excluded by `build_owner_filter`. The two columns involved hold different value shapes: ``` $ psql -U llmproxy -d litellm -t -c \ "SELECT id, unified_object_id FROM \"LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable\" WHERE file_purpose='batch' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3;" d11caa62-27a6-4279-adb2-e70b7f4aa1fe | bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTttb2RlbF9pZDo0ZDhhNWVmMGY2Y2M5OTZkMmEwYzlmYmEzYTMxMzQ5Mjg0OTYxNWNhM2E2YmJjNGRjOTcyMDQ0Mjg4MTBmMjk0O2xsbV9iYXRjaF9pZDpiYXRjaF8yMDI2MDgxNy0wNTU4LjMyMA d0fc3f0d-4edd-458a-bfe6-601f98a816f6 | bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTttb2RlbF9pZDo0ZDhhNWVmMGY2Y2M5OTZkMmEwYzlmYmEzYTMxMzQ5Mjg0OTYxNWNhM2E2YmJjNGRjOTcyMDQ0Mjg4MTBmMjk0O2xsbV9iYXRjaF9pZDpiYXRjaF8yMDI2MDgxNy0wNTU3LjAxOQ 32e97180-688a-4e74-a757-bcf9924915af | bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTttb2RlbF9pZDo2MzA0N2NjOGU1MzU3MWJmMDRiY2E4ODZiYjhiNzljNjg5MmQ5OWIwMjEwZGIzMTdhM2Y3MTVmM2EzZjYyMDQ0O2xsbV9iYXRjaF9pZDpiYXRjaF8yMDI2MDgxMy0xMDMxLjMzNA ``` `id` holds a UUID. `unified_object_id`, the value returned to the caller as `id`, holds a base64 string. The `{"gt": after}` filter is applied to `id`. --- ### User Flow **Before a (hypothetical) fix: an analyst exporting a quarter of batch jobs receives repeated rows and a loop that does not end** 1. They send `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/batches?limit=10` and receive 10 batches 2. They take the `id` of the last item and send `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/batches?limit=10&after=<that id>` 3. The second page returns 10 batches, of which 8 appeared on page 1 4. Every page reports `"has_more": true`, so their loop continues requesting pages 5. They stop it after 15 pages. It has collected 150 rows containing 16 distinct batches, and 83 of the account's 99 batches appear on no page 6. Every call in the sequence returned `200` **After a (hypothetical) fix: each page continues from the previous one and the loop ends** 1. They send `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/batches?limit=10` and receive 10 batches 2. They take the `id` of the last item and send `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/batches?limit=10&after=<that id>` 3. The second page returns 10 batches, none of which appeared on page 1 4. On the tenth page `"has_more"` is `false`, so their loop exits 5. The 10 pages together contain all 99 batches, each once 6. Every call in the sequence returned `200` --- ### Proof the bug occurs **Version**: `litellm 1.94.3`, image digest `sha256:b7d979bac2a9e8fbb7d55272ef5f1f4a08ab365de8f78b1800834ca718d4c941`. No provider call is made on this path. **Config the proxy ran with** ```yaml model_list: - model_name: gpt-5-batch litellm_params: model: azure/gpt-5-batch-2025-08-07 api_base: os.environ/AZURE_API_BASE api_key: os.environ/AZURE_API_KEY general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL ``` **Commands and their full output** Total from a single request: ``` $ curl -s 'http://localhost:4000/v1/batches?limit=100' -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_KEY" \ | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print("total:", len(json.load(sys.stdin)["data"]))' total: 99 ``` Walk at `limit=10`, passing the previous page's last `id` as `after`, capped at 15 pages: ``` === paginated walk, limit=10, following the id the API returns === page 1: returned=10 has_more=True page 2: returned=10 has_more=True page 3: returned=10 has_more=True page 4: returned=10 has_more=True page 5: returned=10 has_more=True page 6: returned=10 has_more=True page 7: returned=10 has_more=True page 8: returned=10 has_more=True page 9: returned=10 has_more=True page 10: returned=10 has_more=True page 11: returned=10 has_more=True page 12: returned=10 has_more=True page 13: returned=10 has_more=True page 14: returned=10 has_more=True page 15: returned=10 has_more=True true total (single page): 99 rows returned by walk: 150 distinct rows in walk: 16 DUPLICATES: 134 NEVER SEEN by the walk: 83 ``` Two consecutive pages at `limit=3`: ``` page1 ids (first 20 chars): ['bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt', 'bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt', 'bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt'] cursor sent as after= bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt (len 166) page2 ids (first 20 chars): ['bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt', 'bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt', 'bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtt'] page2 identical to page1? False overlap count: 2 of 3 ``` The `id` values returned to the caller are 166-character base64 strings. The `id` column the `after` filter compares against holds UUIDs, per the psql output above. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.94.3

signal.title: feat(proxy/guardrails): add native Gate/Prove ActionBoundary guardrail and Action Ledger exporter
signal.text: ### Summary Adds a native Gate/Prove `ActionGateGuardrail` and cryptographic `ActionLedger` plugin for LiteLLM Proxy under `litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_hooks/action_gate/`. ### Problem Solved As enterprises deploy LiteLLM Proxy across autonomous multi-agent systems and tool-calling models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex AI), platform engineering and security teams require: 1. **Zero-Trust Action Boundaries**: Enforcing `never_equate_intent_to_approval` to prevent un-gated, unconfirmed state-mutating tool invocations. 2. **Emergency Kill Switch**: Immediate cessation of proxy traffic via `AAG_KILL_SWITCH` environment variables or `artifacts/KILL` file triggers. 3. **Cryptographic Action Ledger**: Generating immutable, SHA-256 hash-chained JSONL receipts satisfying NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 audit logging (`AU-2`, `AU-3`, `AU-12`) for SOC 2 Type II and ISO 42001 compliance reviews. ### Guardrail Features Added - `ActionGateGuardrail`: - `async_pre_call_hook`: Intercepts emergency kill switches and validates tool execution boundaries. - `async_post_call_success_hook`: Extracts LLM tool calls and records cryptographic hash-chained audit receipts. - `verify_ledger_integrity()`: Validates cryptographic SHA-256 chain integrity across all recorded events. ### Testing & Validation - Added `tests/test_action_gate_guardrail.py` validating pre-call validation, post-call ledger recording, and cryptographic hash-chain integrity (3/3 tests passing). ### Upstream & Commercial Context Maintained by [A2Z SOC](https://a2zsoc.com) for enterprise AI proxy governance, FinOps cost guardrails, and compliance audit readiness. signal.title: [Bug]: service_tier=priority silently billed at default rate for gpt-4o/gpt-4.1 family (missing pricing keys on dated-snapshot model entries)
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? ## Actual behaviour For `gpt-4o`, `gpt-4o-mini`, `gpt-4.1`, and `gpt-4.1-mini`, sending `service_tier="priority"` is accepted by OpenAI (the response correctly echoes back `response.service_tier == "priority"`), but the cost LiteLLM computes (`x-litellm-response-cost` header / spend logs) is identical to the **default**-tier cost, not the priority-tier cost. By contrast, the same test against `gpt-5`, `gpt-5-mini`, `gpt-5.4`, `gpt-5.4-mini` correctly applies priority/flex pricing. ## Live verification (thunk-prod proxy, tiny `max_tokens=5` calls) | model | tier | prompt/completion tokens | reported cost | expected cost (priority rate) | |---|---|---|---|---| | gpt-4o-mini | priority | 9 / 2 | 2.55e-06 | 4.25e-06 | | gpt-4o | priority | 9 / 1 | 3.25e-05 | 5.525e-05 | | gpt-4.1 | priority | 9 / 1 | 2.6e-05 | 4.55e-05 | | gpt-4.1-mini | priority | 9 / 1 | 5.2e-06 | 9.1e-06 | In every case the "reported cost" exactly matches what default-tier pricing would produce for the same token counts, confirming priority pricing was silently not applied. ## Root cause `model_prices_and_context_window_backup.json` defines `input_cost_per_token_priority` / `output_cost_per_token_priority` on the **alias** entries (`gpt-4o`, `gpt-4o-mini`, `gpt-4.1`, `gpt-4.1-mini`) but **not** on the **dated-snapshot** entries that OpenAI actually echoes back in `response.model` (`gpt-4o-2024-08-06`, `gpt-4o-2024-11-20`, `gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18`, `gpt-4.1-2025-04-14`, `gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14`): ``` gpt-4o priority_in=4.25e-06 priority_out=1.7e-05 gpt-4o-2024-08-06 priority_in=None priority_out=None gpt-4o-2024-11-20 priority_in=None priority_out=None gpt-4o-mini priority_in=2.5e-07 priority_out=1e-06 gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 priority_in=None priority_out=None gpt-4.1 priority_in=3.5e-06 priority_out=1.4e-05 gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 priority_in=None priority_out=None gpt-4.1-mini priority_in=7e-07 priority_out=2.8e-06 gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 priority_in=None priority_out=None ``` `cost_calculator.py`'s model-name resolution (`_select_model_name_for_cost_calc` / `potential_model_names`, around lines 688-692 and 1115-1131) prefers the dated snapshot name echoed by OpenAI over the caller-supplied alias when looking up pricing. `litellm_core_utils/llm_cost_calc/utils.py`'s `_get_cost_per_unit` (~lines 349-388) then silently falls back to base (non-priority) pricing when the `_priority` key is absent on the resolved (dated-snapshot) model_info entry — no error or warning is raised. For `gpt-5`/`gpt-5-mini`, both the alias **and** the dated-snapshot entry (`gpt-5-2025-08-07`, `gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07`) carry `_priority` keys, so the same lookup path resolves correctly there — confirming this is a pricing-data completeness gap, not a code-path difference between model families. ## Expected behaviour Priority-tier cost should be applied whenever the model actually served the request at `priority` tier, regardless of whether the model resolves via alias or dated-snapshot name. Either: 1. Add `input_cost_per_token_priority`/`output_cost_per_token_priority` (and `_flex` where applicable) to the dated-snapshot JSON entries for these models, or 2. Make the cost-key fallback in `llm_cost_calc/utils.py` fall back from a dated-snapshot entry to its alias entry (not straight to base pricing) when a tier-specific key is missing. ## Impact Any proxy user billing `service_tier=priority` traffic on `gpt-4o`, `gpt-4o-mini`, `gpt-4.1`, or `gpt-4.1-mini` is under-reporting spend — potentially significantly, since priority pricing is ~1.7-2x the default rate on these models while actual OpenAI billing is presumably at the priority rate. ### Relevant log output _N/A — reproducible via `x-litellm-response-cost` response header, see table above._ ### Are you a ML Ops Team? - [ ] Yes ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? Reproduced against a production proxy; latest `main` as of 2026-08-15 has the same gap in `model_prices_and_context_window_backup.json`. ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_
