signal.title: feat: add tiyuvta as an OpenAI-compatible provider
signal.text: Adds `tiyuvta` to the JSON provider registry, following `litellm/llms/openai_like/README.md`. Replaces #37141, which I opened against `main` before reading the branch policy — `Verify PR source branch` correctly rejected it and pointed fork contributions here. ```json "tiyuvta": { "base_url": "https://api.tiyuvta.ai/v1", "api_key_env": "TIYUVTA_API_KEY", "api_base_env": "TIYUVTA_API_BASE", "supported_endpoints": ["/v1/chat/completions", "/v1/completions"] } ``` **What it is.** A prepaid OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint I run, serving Qwen3.8-27B at its full 262,144-token context on [memra](https://github.com/avifenesh/memra), an open-source Rust + CUDA engine. Docs: <https://inference.tiyuvta.ai/docs>. **Two files, because `code-quality` checks they agree.** The registry entry alone fails provider-documentation validation — every `openai_like` provider must also appear in `provider_endpoints_support.json`. Inserted there as text, so the diff is additions only rather than a reformat of the file. ## The support matrix row is measured, not asserted Every field was run against the live endpoint with `litellm 1.97.0` and a real key, with the provider entry from this PR patched into the installed registry: | field | value | how it was determined | |---|---|---| | `chat_completions` | **true** | `litellm.completion(...)` → `ok`; streaming returns content plus 110 `reasoning_content` chunks | | `messages` | **true** | `await litellm.anthropic_messages(...)` → Anthropic-shaped content blocks, with the model's reasoning mapped into a `thinking` block | | `responses` | **true** | `litellm.responses(...).output_text` → `ok` | | `embeddings` | false | `LiteLLMUnknownProvider: Unmapped LLM provider for this endpoint` | | `image_generations` | false | returns an `ImageResponse` with `data: []`, zero usage, `custom_llm_provider=None` — it never reaches a provider. Worth flagging: this path returns an empty object instead of raising, so a naive probe reads it as success | | `audio_transcriptions`, `audio_speech`, `rerank` | false | `ValueError: 'tiyuvta' is not a valid LlmProviders` | | `moderations`, `batches` | false | fall through to OpenAI credentials; batches additionally needs a files API this endpoint does not have | | `a2a` | false | no `a2a` entry point exists in litellm 1.97.0 | `tool_calls` and `response_format: json_schema` were checked in the same pass and both behave — a tool call came back as `{"city":"Haifa"}` for `get_weather`, and the schema request returned valid conforming JSON. An earlier revision of this PR declared `messages` and `responses` false because I had not tested the bridge. That was the wrong way to settle it, so I ran the calls; the second commit flips both with the evidence above. **No `param_mappings`.** Most entries here map `max_completion_tokens` → `max_tokens`. This endpoint already accepts `max_completion_tokens` as an alias server-side, with a test covering it, so the mapping would be a no-op. **One note for reviewers testing this by hand**: the model reasons before it answers, so a small `max_tokens` is consumed entirely by reasoning and returns empty content with a 200. My first measurement pass did exactly that and looked like a silent failure. 400 tokens is enough to see content.

signal.title: feat(realtime): add realtime_audio guardrail hook with per-frame holdback
signal.text: ## The gap Realtime guardrails today receive only the provider's own transcription, via `run_realtime_guardrails(transcript: str)` → `apply_guardrail(inputs={"texts": [transcript], "images": []})`. And the only enforcement available mid-session is `end_session_after_n_fails`, which closes the connection. That leaves two things a voice guardrail can't do: 1. **Apply its own speech models.** `GenericGuardrailAPIInputs` carries `texts` and `images` only, so a guardrail inherits the provider's transcription quality, timing and vocabulary rather than transcribing itself. 2. **Suppress a fragment of speech.** Blocking hangs up the call. There's no way to withhold one frame and let the conversation continue. ## What this adds The audio counterpart to the `stream_holdback_chars` pattern already in `GenericGuardrailAPIInputs`. - **`GuardrailAudioFrame`** + an `audio` key on `GenericGuardrailAPIInputs`. The sample rate travels *with the frame*, because a realtime session carries different rates in each direction (commonly 16 kHz client mic, 24 kHz model output) and so it can't be assumed per session. Read from `input_audio_format` / `output_audio_format` when the session declares them, with per-direction defaults otherwise. - **`GuardrailEventHooks.realtime_audio`**, so opting in is explicit and separate from the transcript hook. - **`run_realtime_audio_guardrails()`** on both directions: - client `input_audio_buffer.append` frames are screened in `client_ack_messages` before being relayed upstream; - model audio deltas are screened in `_send_event_to_client`, which already funnels every backend event, so the raw and `provider_config` paths (Gemini/Vertex) behave identically without duplicating logic. - A withheld frame is **dropped while the session stays open**. ## Costs nothing when unused `_has_realtime_audio_guardrails()` gates the whole path, so a session with only text guardrails does no extra parse, no await before forwarding, and takes no added latency. This mirrors how `_has_audio_transcription_guardrails()` already scopes the VAD auto-response behaviour. A guardrail that raises a non-block error is logged and skipped rather than silently discarding the caller's audio — same contract as the text path. ## Tests 10 new cases in `tests/test_litellm/litellm_core_utils/test_realtime_audio_guardrails.py`: - frame contents (speaker, encoding, sequence, round-tripped payload) - per-direction default sample rates - declared session formats overriding those defaults - per-speaker monotonic sequencing - a model frame withheld without the session closing - both beta (`response.audio.delta`) and GA (`response.output_audio.delta`) spellings - non-audio events forwarded untouched - missing/empty `delta` not screened - a transcript-only guardrail never handed audio, and `_has_realtime_audio_guardrails()` false for it - a crashing guardrail not causing audio to be dropped `tests/test_litellm/litellm_core_utils/test_realtime_streaming.py` (101 tests) unaffected. No new `ruff-strict-budget` findings; `ruff format` clean. ## Notes for reviewers - Happy to change the hook name, the frame shape, or split the two directions into separate hooks if you'd prefer a different surface. - Left as draft because I'd like your read on the shape before I add docs to `docs/my-website/docs/proxy/guardrails/` and a realtime-audio example. - Motivation: building a voice guardrail that needs first-party transcription and the ability to withhold a fragment without dropping the call. Happy to share more detail if useful.

signal.title: feat: add GPUStack embedding and rerank support
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - `gpustack/...` models are not recognized - Embedding and rerank require provider impersonation How it solves it: - Adds native GPUStack embedding routing - Adds native GPUStack rerank routing - Preserves owner-prefixed model route IDs - Honors caller authorization case-insensitively ## User Flow Before: a developer cannot select GPUStack directly for embedding or rerank 1. They configure `gpustack/tiny-embed` or `gpustack/tiny-rerank` 2. They send `POST http://localhost:4000/v1/embeddings` or `POST http://localhost:4000/rerank` 3. LiteLLM returns a provider-mapping error before contacting GPUStack After: the same configuration routes requests to GPUStack's native endpoints 1. They set `GPUSTACK_API_BASE` and `GPUSTACK_API_KEY` 2. They configure `gpustack/tiny-embed` or `gpustack/tiny-rerank` 3. They send the same embedding or rerank request 4. LiteLLM calls `/v1/embeddings` or `/v1/rerank` 5. OpenAI embedding data or rerank results return normally ## Relevant issues Related to #25833. `no_issue_rationale`: #25833 covers general GPUStack onboarding; no dedicated issue covers native embedding and rerank routing. Documentation pairing: [BerriAI/litellm-docs#911](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm-docs/pull/911) documents the native `gpustack/` embedding/rerank routes plus `GPUSTACK_API_BASE` and `GPUSTACK_API_KEY`. The existing docs PR BerriAI/litellm-docs#629 covers generic Custom OpenAI chat configuration instead, so it does not satisfy this provider's native contract. The `documentation` and `code-quality` env-key checks read `litellm-docs` main and remain red until #911 merges. ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all locally runnable CI/CD checks - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup: GPUStack v2.2.3 on CPU, `tiny-embed` backed by `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, and `tiny-rerank` backed by `cross-encoder/ms-marco-TinyBERT-L-2-v2`. ### Before (973329e9864154d429a7d739fb6a552fe03a9b3e) 1. Called `litellm.embedding(model="gpustack/tiny-embed", ...)` against the live GPUStack server. 2. Observed `BadRequestError` with provider mapping missing before any inference call. ### After (fe1c78dd23122a31c192f1a4436584080f102437) 1. Called sync embedding through the live GPUStack gateway. 2. Observed `PASS`, 384 dimensions, and 10 total tokens. 3. Called async embedding through the same live GPUStack gateway. 4. Observed `PASS`, 384 dimensions, and 12 total tokens. Rerank live verification reached a GPUStack v2.2.3 infrastructure blocker: the managed reranker instance was `running`, its route reported `ready_targets=1`, and the runner answered its private `/rerank` endpoint, but the public gateway returned 404 for `/v1/rerank` and `/v2/rerank`; the direct GPUStack API handler returned 503 while forwarding to the worker's missing `/v1/rerank`. The provider's public GPUStack request/response contract remains covered by sync/async HTTP acceptance tests, but this local run is not represented as a successful public-gateway E2E. ## Testing - Focused plus related embedding/rerank regression suite: 38 passed - Lazy-import regression suite: 15 passed - Provider-resolution benchmark tests: 4 passed - Ruff format/check: passed - basedpyright: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes - compileall and `git diff --check`: passed - Independent fail-closed review: passed with no security, logic, test-gap, or scope findings - Strict Ruff budget and provider-folder documentation gate: passed after CI remediation - GPUStack env-key extraction is fully covered by the page in BerriAI/litellm-docs#911 `tests/local_testing/test_provider_specific_config.py` was also attempted, but its session-level fake OpenAI endpoint at `127.0.0.1:8190` did not become healthy; selected cases were blocked during fixture setup before assertions ran. ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats (if any) - GPUStack v2.2.3 local rerank forwarding blocked live gateway proof ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check routing, URLs, payloads, responses, usage, environment configuration, async paths, owner-prefixed IDs, and authorization precedence

signal.title: fix(anthropic): handle missing text field in content_block_start chunks
signal.text:
Some Anthropic-compatible providers emit content_block_start events for text blocks without the optional ext field - sending {"type": "text"} instead of {"type": "text", "text": ""}. This causes a KeyError: 'text' crash in ModelResponseIterator.chunk_parser.

The fix is a one-character change: use .get("text", "") instead of ["text"] so the stream degrades gracefully and downstream content_block_delta chunks deliver the actual content as normal.

Added a unit test that reproduces the exact failing case.

Fixes #28067

signal.title: Proxy UI shows 'Request/Response Data Not Available' even with store_prompts_in_spend_logs=true (data stored in proxy_server_request, not messages)
signal.text: ### What happened? After upgrading LiteLLM proxy, the Spend Logs UI frequently shows: > Request/Response Data Not Available with instructions to enable: ```yaml general_settings: store_model_in_db: true store_prompts_in_spend_logs: true ``` But these settings are already enabled, and prompt data is still being stored (just not in the expected field). ### Environment - LiteLLM image: `docker.litellm.ai/berriai/litellm:main-latest` - LiteLLM package version in container: `1.82.1` - Postgres: `15.17-alpine` - Redis: `7.4-alpine` ### Relevant config ```yaml general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY api_key: os.environ/LITELLM_API_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL store_model_in_db: true store_prompts_in_spend_logs: true ``` ### Reproduction 1. Start proxy with the above config. 2. Send a normal request via `/v1/chat/completions`. 3. Open Spend Logs UI and click request details. 4. Banner appears for many rows saying request/response data is unavailable. ### What I observed in DB For a fresh request (`request_id = 0852eecf-87a5-40a9-a567-dd552a69ce90`): - `messages` is `{}` - `proxy_server_request` is populated (contains input messages) - `response` is populated Example query result: ```sql select request_id, ("messages"::text<>'{}') as has_messages, ("proxy_server_request"::text<>'{}') as has_proxy_req, ("response"::text<>'{}') as has_response from "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" where "request_id"='0852eecf-87a5-40a9-a567-dd552a69ce90'; -- has_messages=false, has_proxy_req=true, has_response=true ``` So prompts are stored in `proxy_server_request`, but UI appears to rely on `messages` for request details, leading to misleading banner text. ### Expected behavior If prompt storage is enabled and prompt exists in spend logs (whether in `messages` or `proxy_server_request`), the UI should show it and not display the enable-storage banner. ### Actual behavior UI banner says storage is not enabled / request data unavailable, even when request payload is present in `proxy_server_request`. Could this be a regression in the Spend Logs UI mapping after recent versions?

signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - LiteLLM cannot route requests to RunInfra's OpenAI compatible API - RunInfra model prices are unknown, so spend tracking reads zero How it solves it: - Registers `runinfra` as a JSON-configured openai_like provider - Adds cost map entries for RunInfra's four hosted models ## User Flow Before: a developer with a RunInfra API key cannot use it through LiteLLM 1. The request goes to POST https://api.runinfra.ai/v1/chat/completions with their bearer key and returns 200 with the assistant message 3. `litellm.completion_cost(response)` returns non-zero spend derived from the new cost map prices ## Relevant issues ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix All proofs below were captured at commit `18690ea835` against the live RunInfra API through a local proxy started from this branch, no mocks, real spend ```bash cat > runinfra_config.yaml <<'YAML' model_list: - model_name: deepseek-v4-flash litellm_params: model: runinfra/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 api_key: os.environ/RUNINFRA_API_KEY general_settings: master_key: sk-1234 YAML litellm --config runinfra_config.yaml --port 4000 ``` Non-streaming completion through the proxy: ```bash curl http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" \ -d '{"model": "deepseek-v4-flash", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello"}]}' ``` ```json {"id":"chatcmpl-964932abcee434d9","created":1786838953,"model":"deepseek-v4-flash","object":"chat.completion","choices":[{"finish_reason":"stop","index":0,"message":{"content":"Hello!","role":"assistant","reasoning_content":"We need answer user asks \"Say hello\" simple. Docs page: BerriAI/litellm-docs#903 - `runinfra/Inferact/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-NVFP4` omits response schema support on purpose - Cache read pricing listed only where RunInfra offers it - The provider's pages for `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` and the Nemotron model currently display a promotional free window ($0.00 through 2026-08-18) alongside their standing rates; the cost map lists the standing non-promotional rates, which is what spend tracking should use ### Final Attestation - signal.title: feat(melious): add Melious as a provider
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - `melious/*` model names do not resolve at all - Reaching Melious needs a hand-wired base URL per deployment - Its two API surfaces need two different base URLs - Spend reads zero without hand-pasted per-token prices How it solves it: - Registers `melious` across the provider map - Serves `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages` natively - Ships cost-map entries for 17 flagship chat models ## User Flow Before: a developer routing to Melious wires a base URL into every deployment, and a second, different one for the Anthropic surface 1. They add a deployment with `model: openai/glm-5.1`, `api_base: https://api.melious.ai/v1`, and their Melious key 2. They send POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions with `"model": "glm-5.1"` and get a normal completion back 3. They want Claude Code on the same account, so they add a second deployment with `model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4` and `api_base: https://api.melious.ai`, this time without the `/v1` 4. Whenever either base URL carries the wrong suffix the call returns `NotFoundError: The requested resource was not found`, which never says which surface was wrong 5. Every response header reads `x-litellm-response-cost: 0.0` until they look up per-token prices and paste them into each deployment After: naming the model is the whole configuration, and one key covers both surfaces 1. They export `MELIOUS_API_KEY` and add a deployment with `model: melious/glm-5.1`, no `api_base` 2. They send POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions with `"model": "glm-5.1"` and get the same completion back 3. For Claude Code they add `model: melious/claude-sonnet-4`, again with no `api_base` 4. They send POST http://localhost:4000/v1/messages and get an Anthropic-shaped response, streaming events included 5. signal.title: [Feature]: Support Azure AI Foundry Agents v2 (Responses API with agent_reference)
signal.text: ## Feature Request ### What is your use case? We are integrating with Microsoft Foundry Agent Service. We've deployed agents using the new Foundry Agents v2 experience, which uses the Responses API with `agent_reference` (referencing agents by name and version) rather than the deprecated Assistants API (thread/run pattern with `asst_*` IDs). The current `azure_ai/agents/{agent_id}` route in LiteLLM implements the old Assistants API pattern, which: 1. Requires agent IDs beginning with `asst_` (but the new Foundry experience does not surface these IDs) 2. Uses the thread → message → run → poll flow (but the new Foundry Agents v2 uses `openai_client.responses.create()` with an `agent_reference` in `extra_body`) Microsoft has [deprecated the Assistants API](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry-classic/openai/how-to/assistant) with retirement set for **August 26, 2026**. ### The new API pattern From the Azure AI Foundry getting-started code: ```python from azure.ai.projects import AIProjectClient from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential project_client = AIProjectClient( endpoint="https://<resource>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project>", credential=DefaultAzureCredential(), ) openai_client = project_client.get_openai_client() response = openai_client.responses.create( input=[{"role": "user", "content": "Tell me what you can help with."}], extra_body={ "agent_reference": { "name": "my-agent-name", "version": "1", "type": "agent_reference", } }, ) ``` Key differences from the current `azure_ai/agents` implementation: - **Endpoint**: Project-level (`https://<resource>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project>`) - **API**: Responses API (`/openai/responses`), not Assistants/Threads API - **Agent identification**: By `name` + `version` via `agent_reference` in extra_body, not by `asst_*` ID - **Auth**: Azure AD (Entra ID) bearer token — same as current implementation ### Proposed model format ``` azure_ai/agents/<agent_name>:<version> ``` For example: `azure_ai/agents/my-agent-name:1` ### Reference docs - [Agent identity concepts in Microsoft Foundry](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/agent-identity) - [Authentication and authorization in Microsoft Foundry](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/authentication-authorization-foundry) - [Assistants API deprecation notice](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry-classic/openai/how-to/assistant) ### Are you a LiteLLM Enterprise customer? No

signal.title: Add tiyuvta as an OpenAI-compatible provider
signal.text: Adds `tiyuvta` to `litellm/llms/openai_like/providers.json`, following that directory's README. ```json "tiyuvta": { "base_url": "https://api.tiyuvta.ai/v1", "api_key_env": "TIYUVTA_API_KEY", "api_base_env": "TIYUVTA_API_BASE", "supported_endpoints": ["/v1/chat/completions", "/v1/completions"] } ``` **What it is.** A prepaid OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint I run, serving Qwen3.8-27B at its full 262,144-token context on [memra](https://github.com/avifenesh/memra), an open-source Rust + CUDA engine. Docs: <https://inference.tiyuvta.ai/docs>. `GET https://api.tiyuvta.ai/v1/models` is public and answers 200. **No `param_mappings`.** Most entries here map `max_completion_tokens` → `max_tokens`. This endpoint already accepts `max_completion_tokens` as an alias for `max_tokens` server-side, with a test covering it, so the mapping would be a no-op and is left out rather than added for symmetry. **`supported_endpoints` lists only what is actually served**: chat completions and completions. No `/v1/responses`, `/v1/messages` or `/v1/embeddings` — declaring those would make `JSONProviderRegistry.supports_responses_api()` answer yes for an endpoint that has none. Streaming, tool calls, `response_format` (`json_object` and `json_schema`), and separated reasoning output all work through the standard Chat Completions shape. JSON validated: parses, 27 providers, no duplicate keys.

signal.title: ResponsesAPIResponse.created_at should be Optional[int] - Azure returns null for in-progress/queued responses
signal.text: ## Description `ResponsesAPIResponse` in `litellm/types/llms/openai.py` declares `created_at: int` as a required field. However, Azure OpenAI's GET /v1/responses/{id} returns `created_at: null` when the response is still `in_progress` or `queued`. This causes a `pydantic.ValidationError` in `transform_get_response_api_response` → wrapped as `APIConnectionError` → HTTP 500 returned to the caller, defeating Azure's intended polling semantics (which should return HTTP 200 with an in-progress object). ## Steps to reproduce 1. Submit a response creation request to Azure OpenAI (e.g. model `gpt-5.1`) 2. Immediately poll GET /v1/responses/{id} 3. Azure returns: ```json {"id": "...", "created_at": null, "output": null, "status": "queued"} ``` 4. `ResponsesAPIResponse(**payload)` raises ValidationError ## Expected behavior `created_at` should be `Optional[int] = None` (similar to `model`, `status`, and other fields), or `transform_get_response_api_response` should normalize null values before constructing the model. ## Context We're running LiteLLM v1.92.0 proxying Azure OpenAI. When polling queued/in-progress responses, Azure returns `created_at: null` along with other nullable fields (`id`, `output`). Two of those fields have already been patched downstream but `created_at` still causes failures. Related upstream issue for nullable fields in streaming: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/20570 ## Observed error ``` pydantic.ValidationError: 1 validation error for ResponsesAPIResponse created_at Input should be a valid integer [type=int_type, input_value=None, input_type=NoneType] ```

signal.title: ResponsesAPIResponse.created_at should be Optional[int] - Azure returns null for in-progress/queued responses
signal.text:
## Description

`ResponsesAPIResponse` in `litellm/types/llms/openai.py` declares `created_at: int` as a required field. However, Azure OpenAI's GET /v1/responses/{id} returns `created_at: null` when the response is still in_progress or queued.

This causes a `pydantic.ValidationError` in `transform_get_response_api_response` → wrapped as `APIConnectionError` → HTTP 500 returned to the caller, defeating Azure's intended polling semantics (which should return HTTP 200 with an in-progress object).

## Steps to reproduce

1. Submit a response creation request to Azure OpenAI (e.g. model `gpt-5.1`)
2. Immediately poll GET /v1/responses/{id}
3. Azure returns: `{"id": "...", "created_at": null, "output": null, "status": "queued"}`
4. `ResponsesAPIResponse(**payload)` raises ValidationError

## Expected behavior

`created_at` should be `Optional[int] = None` (similar to `model`, `status`, and other fields), or `transform_get_response_api_response` should normalize null values before constructing the model.

## Context

We're running LiteLLM v1.92.0 proxying Azure OpenAI. When polling queued/in-progress responses, Azure returns `created_at: null` along with other nullable fields (`id`, `output`). We've patched two of those fields but `created_at` still causes failures.

Related upstream issue for nullable fields in streaming: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/20570

## Observed error

```
pydantic.ValidationError: 1 validation error for ResponsesAPIResponse
created_at
 Input should be a valid integer [type=int_type, input_value=None, input_type=NoneType]
```

signal.title: fix: enable reasoning_effort for Mistral reasoning models
signal.text: ## Summary Enable `reasoning_effort` for Mistral chat models that Mistral documents as supporting it, not just the models whose name contains `magistral`. ## Problem `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `model=mistral-medium-3-5` and `reasoning_effort` fails with: ``` litellm.UnsupportedParamsError: mistral does not support parameters: ['reasoning_effort'], for model=mistral-medium-3-5 ``` This happens because the Mistral chat transformation only adds `reasoning_effort`/`thinking` to the supported param set when the model name contains `"magistral"`. `mistral-medium-3-5` does not match that check, so LiteLLM rejects the parameter before it reaches Mistral. ## Why this is a real bug Mistral's own docs state that `mistral-medium-3-5` supports adjustable reasoning via `reasoning_effort`, and that `mistral-small-latest` does as well. Rejecting a parameter that the provider accepts is a translation bug, not a user configuration issue. ## Fix Add a MistralConfig helper that decides whether a Mistral chat model supports reasoning params according to Mistral's documented reasoning model set, and use it in both: - `get_supported_openai_params`, so `reasoning_effort`/`thinking` are accepted - `map_openai_params`, so they are forwarded for the same models At minimum, this enables the parameters for `magistral-*`, `mistral-medium-3-5`, and `mistral-small-latest`, without enabling `reasoning_effort` for every `mistral-*` model by default. ## Test plan This is a request-translation/allowlist fix, so it can be verified without hitting the real Mistral API: - `MistralConfig.get_supported_openai_params("mistral-medium-3-5")` now includes `reasoning_effort` - `MistralConfig.get_supported_openai_params("mistral-small-latest")` now includes `reasoning_effort` - `MistralConfig.get_supported_openai_params("magistral-medium-latest")` still includes `reasoning_effort` - Non-reasoning Mistral models such as legacy `mistral-7b` variants do not gain `reasoning_effort` from this change ## References Fixes #36407

signal.title: fix: hold references to the background tasks in auth_checks
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Ten `create_task()` results discarded in `auth_checks.py` - One is a **database write**, not telemetry — an SSO binding - The loop only weakly references tasks, so they can vanish mid-flight How it solves it: - Holds each task in a module-level set, drops it in a done callback - Same pattern the repo already uses in three other places - No control flow change ## Relevant issues None found. ## The one that is not telemetry In `get_user_object_from_db_or_cache`, when a user is matched by email during SSO, the `sso_user_id` binding is persisted in the background: ```python if response is not None and sso_user_id is not None: # update sso_user_id asyncio.create_task( # background task to update user with sso id UserRepository(prisma_client).table.update( where={"user_id": response.user_id}, data={"sso_user_id": sso_user_id}, ) ) ``` The task is discarded, and [the event loop only keeps a weak reference](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html#asyncio.create_task): > Important: Save a reference to the result of this function, to avoid a task disappearing mid-execution. The event loop only keeps weak references to tasks. A task that isn't referenced elsewhere may get garbage collected at any time, even before it's done. If it is collected the login still succeeds, so nothing looks wrong — but the binding is never written. The next login falls back to the email lookup again, and the SSO identity never sticks. No exception, no log line; from the outside it reads like a flaky identity provider. ## The other nine Budget alerts — token, soft, max, organization, team and key budgets. A collected alert simply never fires, so a budget event passes unnoticed. Less severe than a lost write, same root cause. | line | task | |---|---| | 1615 | `UserRepository.table.update` — SSO binding | | 3607, 3711, 3802, 3834, 3998 | `budget_alerts` — token / soft / max / team | | 4116, 4160, 4212, 4350 | `budget_alerts` — key / organization | ## The change ```python _background_tasks: set[asyncio.Task] = set() # mutable-ok: task registry ... _background_task = asyncio.create_task(...) _background_tasks.add(_background_task) _background_task.add_done_callback(_background_tasks.discard) ``` `discard` rather than `remove` so a double callback cannot raise. The set stays bounded by the number of in-flight tasks. **The repo already does this correctly elsewhere**, which is why I treated it as a bug rather than a style preference — `guardrail_hooks/akto/akto.py:85`, `management_helpers/audit_logs.py:142`, `mcp_server/.../oauth_token_store.py:238`. ## Verification ```console $ ruff check litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py # ruff 0.15.3, pinned in pyproject.toml All checks passed! $ ruff format --check litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py 1 file left unchanged $ python scripts/check_type_discipline.py litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py | grep -c LIT 229 # 229 on main too — zero net new $ python -m py_compile litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py ``` No test: the failure is a garbage-collection race, so a test would have to force a GC at a chosen moment and assert a task did *not* vanish — flaky by construction. Happy to add one if you have a shape in mind. Found with an AST scan for `create_task` / `ensure_future` results discarded as bare expression statements (excluding `TaskGroup.create_task`, which does hold strong references). Companion to #35347, which does the same for `RedisCache`; this one is a different file and they are independent.

signal.title: fix(deepseek): honor declared supports_reasoning for non-deepseek providers
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - DeepSeek thinking-mode models on third-party OpenAI-compatible gateways never get `reasoning_content` backfilled in multi-turn chats - Multi-turn conversations fail with HTTP 400 `"The reasoning_content in the thinking mode must be passed back to the API."` How it solves it: - `_thinking_mode_active` now also honors `supports_reasoning` declared in model_cost/model_info - DeepSeek-provider default behavior is preserved; any provider can opt deepseek-backed models into reasoning backfill ## User Flow Before: a developer routes Claude Code to a deepseek-backed model on a third-party OpenAI-compatible gateway (e.g. model group `coding` backed by `openai/deepseek-v4-flash`) 1. They send a multi-turn request to POST /v1/messages with a deepseek thinking-mode model 2. The first turn returns reasoning, but the history sent back omits `reasoning_content` 3. The gateway rejects the request with HTTP 400 and the message above, so the agent's session breaks mid-conversation After: the same multi-turn request succeeds 1. The proxy admin declares `supports_reasoning: true` in the model's model_info 2. They send the same POST /v1/messages with the same history 3. LiteLLM backfills the missing `reasoning_content` placeholder, the gateway accepts it, and the conversation continues normally ## Relevant issues Fixes #27946 ## Linear ticket <!-- N/A --> ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats - Deepseek-provider models keep the original auto-true behavior; no config change needed for them - Users on other providers must declare `supports_reasoning: true` in model_info to opt in ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix ### After (8e8c6ac) #### Multi-turn chat completion through a third-party gateway 1. `python -m pytest tests/litellm/llms/deepseek/chat/test_deepseek_chat_transformation.py::TestDeepSeekThinkingModeActive` → 4 passed 2. signal.title: fix(mcp): tolerate invalid content blocks in tools/call results
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - A single malformed content block fails an entire MCP `tools/call` result - Client returns a raw `ValidationError` traceback instead of any content How it solves it: - Degrade only the invalid content block to text instead of raising - Every valid content block in the result is left untouched ## User Flow Before: a developer calling a tool on a non-compliant upstream MCP server through the gateway gets an error instead of the tool's real output 1. They send a `tools/call` JSON-RPC request for a tool backed by an Azure DevOps MCP server to the gateway's MCP endpoint 2. The upstream server's response includes a resource content item using a relative path instead of a full URI, which the MCP client library rejects 3. The gateway's response comes back with `"isError": true` and a single `text` block containing a raw pydantic `ValidationError` traceback, not the tool's actual output After: the same call returns the tool's real output even though the upstream's response is still not fully spec-compliant 1. They send the same `tools/call` JSON-RPC request for the same tool to the same MCP endpoint 2. The upstream server's response still contains that same non-compliant resource content item 3. The gateway's response now comes back with `"isError": false` and the tool's actual output as `text` content ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [ ] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review The lint/format/unit-test box is left unchecked deliberately: this repo's build backend (`maturin`, compiling `litellm-rust`) requires a local Rust toolchain that wasn't available in the environment this PR was written in, so `make lint` / `make test-unit` could not be run locally. The new test was verified with a standalone script exercising the same `mcp==1.28.1` model classes and the same `_ScriptedUpstream`/`_ScriptedClient` harness logic used in the actual test file, not through `pytest` itself. Flagging this explicitly rather than checking a box I couldn't verify; happy to fix anything CI turns up. ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix This is not the live-proxy curl proof this template normally asks for. A local proxy could not be built for the same Rust-toolchain reason noted above. What follows is real evidence gathered against a live, non-compliant upstream MCP server, plus a real run of this fix's exact logic against that captured payload, at the commit above. **Before (parent commit `423b791ee0395815050998dd73542445350ab792`): the real failure, captured live** An MCP `tools/call` request for a `repo_file` tool backed by an Azure DevOps MCP server (`mcp.dev.azure.com`), sent with a real, valid upstream token, returns this content block verbatim: ```json {"type":"resource","resource":{"uri":"/templates/ev.job/template/docker-compose.yml","mimeType":"text/plain","blob":"dmVyc2lvbjogJzIuNCcK..."}} ``` Feeding that exact block into `mcp==1.28.1`'s `CallToolResult.model_validate` (the same call `ClientSession.call_tool` makes internally) raises: ``` pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 14 validation errors for CallToolResult content.0.TextContent.type Input should be 'text' [type=literal_error, input_value='resource', input_type=str] ... content.0.EmbeddedResource.resource.TextResourceContents.uri Input should be a valid URL, relative URL without a base [type=url_parsing, input_value='/templates/ev.job/template/docker-compose.yml', input_type=str] ... ``` This is exactly the `ValidationError` that `MCPClient.call_tool`'s except-block turns into the `isError: true` text block described above. **After (this PR, commit `3b7d9e74cbd8561bf62041c5888168ec64a0779c`): the same payload, run through the new model** ``` $ python -c " from litellm.experimental_mcp_client.tolerant_result import TolerantCallToolResult payload = {'content': [{'type': 'resource', 'resource': { 'uri': '/templates/ev.job/template/docker-compose.yml', 'mimeType': 'text/plain', 'blob': 'dmVyc2lvbjogJzIuNCcK', }}], 'isError': False} result = TolerantCallToolResult.model_validate(payload) print(result.content[0].type, repr(result.content[0].text)) " text "version: '2.4'\n" ``` No exception. `isError` stays `False`. The content that used to be silently discarded behind a traceback comes through as the actual decoded text. The new test in this PR, `TestCallToolToleratesMalformedContentBlocks::test_relative_uri_resource_degrades_to_text_instead_of_raising`, asserts this same outcome through the real `ClientSession`-derived class and real anyio streams via `_ScriptedUpstream`/`_ScriptedClient`, not a hand-built result object; it could not be executed via `pytest` here for the Rust-toolchain reason above, so this is not a substitute for CI actually running it, only evidence that the logic it exercises behaves as asserted. ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ✅ Test ## Caveats (if any) - `make lint` / `make test-unit` not run locally; blocked on this repo's Rust/maturin build requirement - `TolerantClientSession.call_tool` mirrors `mcp==1.28.1`'s method body verbatim (no override seam exists); a later `mcp` release changing that method won't automatically propagate - Uses `Any`/`Mapping[str, Any]`/`object` for the genuinely untyped external data at this one boundary; flagging in case `reportAny` disagrees ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: fix(caching): guard Redis disconnect when cluster mode has no shared pool
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Every proxy shutdown crashes when Redis cluster mode is on - Billing flush and other teardown steps are skipped - Cluster client and its per-node pools are never released How it solves it: - Skip the shared pool teardown when there is no shared pool - Close the cluster client explicitly, then delegate to the base class ## User Flow Before: an admin running Redis in cluster mode loses part of every shutdown 1. They start the proxy with Redis caching pointed at a cluster-mode endpoint, for example ElastiCache Serverless, which is always cluster mode 2. They send SIGTERM to restart or deploy 3. Shutdown ends with `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'disconnect'`, and uvicorn reports `Application shutdown failed. Exiting.` 4. Everything ordered after the cache teardown never runs, so up to one export interval of billable request counts is dropped on that restart, every restart After: the same restart completes and nothing after the cache teardown is skipped 1. They start the proxy with the same cluster-mode Redis configuration 2. They send SIGTERM to restart or deploy 3. Shutdown completes without raising 4. The billing flush runs, so no export interval is lost across the restart ## Relevant issues Fixes #37137 ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup, a real cluster-mode Redis with all slots served by one node, no mocks: ``` docker run -d --name litellm-redis-cluster -p 7000:7000 redis:7 redis-server --port 7000 \ --cluster-enabled yes --cluster-config-file nodes.conf --cluster-node-timeout 5000 \ --cluster-announce-ip 127.0.0.1 --appendonly no docker exec litellm-redis-cluster redis-cli -p 7000 cluster addslotsrange 0 16383 docker exec litellm-redis-cluster redis-cli -p 7000 cluster info | head -2 # cluster_state:ok # cluster_slots_assigned:16384 ``` `repro.py`, which caches through the real cluster and then shuts the cache down: ```python import asyncio from litellm.caching.redis_cluster_cache import RedisClusterCache async def main() -> None: cache = RedisClusterCache(startup_nodes=[{"host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 7000}]) await cache.async_set_cache("proof:37137", "value-from-litellm") print("cached value:", await cache.async_get_cache("proof:37137")) print("async_redis_conn_pool is:", cache.async_redis_conn_pool) await cache.disconnect() print("shutdown completed cleanly") asyncio.run(main()) ``` ### Before (973329e986) 1. `python repro.py` 2. Output, the cache round trip succeeds and the teardown then raises: ``` cached value: value-from-litellm async_redis_conn_pool is: None Traceback (most recent call last): File "repro.py", line 11, in main await cache.disconnect() File "litellm/caching/redis_cache.py", line 1356, in disconnect await self.async_redis_conn_pool.disconnect(inuse_connections=True) AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'disconnect' ``` ### After (3b3103ff33) 1. `python repro.py` 2. Output, the same round trip succeeds and the teardown now completes: ``` cached value: value-from-litellm async_redis_conn_pool is: None shutdown completed cleanly ``` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Captured at the cache layer, not a full SIGTERM proxy run - Cache teardown in shutdown stays unguarded against other failures - Happy to add that try/except here if you want it ## Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.text: ## Summary - paginate the background `reset_budget_windows()` scans for keys and teams - add a fixed safety batch size plus deterministic ordering for each page - extend the regression tests to cover the paginated behavior ## Why PR #26085 fixes a correctness issue where Prisma rejects `{"budget_limits": {"not": None}}` for nullable JSON fields. signal.title: fix(proxy): avoid invalid Prisma JsonFilter in reset_budget_windows
signal.text: ## Summary - stop using `where={"budget_limits": {"not": None}}` in `reset_budget_windows()` for keys and teams - keep filtering in Python with the existing `if not raw: continue` guard and add a regression test for that behavior - avoid periodic `prisma.errors.MissingRequiredValueError` noise from the background budget reset scheduler ## Reproduction This reproduces on the current LiteLLM codepath even when the database contains **zero** rows with `budget_limits` set. Environment used while debugging: - LiteLLM `1.83.10` - `prisma==0.11.0` - `budget_limits` columns present as nullable `jsonb` - `0` rows in both `LiteLLM_VerificationToken` and `LiteLLM_TeamTable` with non-null `budget_limits` Direct reproduction from the running LiteLLM container: ```python rows = await table.find_many(where={"budget_limits": {"not": None}}) ``` This raises: ```text prisma.errors.MissingRequiredValueError: Unable to match input value to any allowed input type for the field. Parse errors: [`where.budget_limits.not`: A value is required but not set, ...] ``` The failure happens before any matching rows are read from Postgres. In this setup, Prisma's generated `JsonFilter.not` expects a JSON value, not Python `None`, so the query itself is invalid. ## Why this change `reset_budget_windows()` already skips empty values in Python: ```python raw = key.budget_limits if not raw: continue ``` So the safest fix is to fetch keys/teams without the invalid Prisma JSON-null filter and preserve the existing Python-side guard. This keeps behavior the same for rows with real window data while avoiding the scheduler log noise for installations that do not use `budget_limits` at all. ## Validation - confirmed the bug against a live LiteLLM container backed by Postgres with no `budget_limits` rows - rebuilt and redeployed the patched image locally - ran `ResetBudgetJob.reset_budget_windows()` successfully in the deployed container with no `MissingRequiredValueError` - verified recent LiteLLM logs no longer contain `MissingRequiredValueError`, `where.budget_limits.not`, or `Failed to reset budget windows` ## Notes I also added a regression test covering the intended behavior: fetch records without a Prisma JSON null filter and only update rows that actually contain `budget_limits`.

signal.title: feat(mcp): add LazyMCP gateway endpoint
signal.text: ## Title feat(mcp): add LazyMCP gateway endpoint # LazyMCP: Using MCP in Agents Without Filling Context With Tools You Will Not Use ## Short Summary LazyMCP is a compact way to expose MCP servers to agents such as OpenCode. Instead of giving the model every tool from every MCP server at startup, LiteLLM exposes three meta-tools: - `mcp_describe` - `mcp_call` - `mcp_status` With these three tools, the agent can discover servers and schemas on demand, and execute real tools when needed. The practical difference is that the model does not pay the context cost of hundreds of tools before knowing which one it actually needs. ## The Problem With Direct MCP MCP is powerful because it lets agents connect to external tools: memory systems, browsers, search engines, databases, GitHub, internal systems, and more. The issue appears when the number of MCP servers grows. In a direct configuration, the agent receives the full tool list. Each tool usually includes: - name, - description, - parameters, - JSON schema, - examples or metadata, - usage constraints. That is fine if you have three or four tools. But if you have twenty MCP servers and hundreds of tools, the initial prompt can be filled with information that may never be used. In OpenCode, this is especially visible. The agent needs context to read code, understand instructions, inspect diffs, review errors, and reason about the task. If a large part of the context is occupied by irrelevant tool schemas, the model works with more noise and less useful space. ## The LazyMCP Idea LazyMCP changes when tool information is delivered. With direct MCP: ```text Agent -> receives all tools and all schemas -> decides what to use ``` With LazyMCP: ```text Agent -> receives 3 meta-tools -> discovers what it needs -> executes what it needs ``` The agent starts with a minimal interface: ```text mcp_status mcp_describe mcp_call ``` Then it can ask: ```json {"server":"memory"} ``` or even: ```json {"server":"memory","tool":"memory-find"} ``` Only then does it receive the input schema for the tool it needs. ## Comparison in OpenCode The best way to explain this is visually. ### Direct MCP The agent sees a large tool list from the first turn. Many tools may be unrelated to the current task. Conceptual example: ```text memory-find memory-store github-list-issues github-create-pr browser-navigate browser-click qdrant-search calendar-create-event drive-search ... ``` Each tool brings its schema. The cost is paid every time, even if the agent only uses one tool. Example of a simple request using 96K out of 262K context because direct MCP loads the full tool catalog up front. ### LazyMCP The agent sees this: ```text mcp_status mcp_describe mcp_call ``` When it needs memory, it asks about memory. When it needs GitHub, it asks about GitHub. When it needs to execute a tool, it calls `mcp_call`. This reduces initial context and helps the model focus on the task. Example of the same simple request using 24K out of 262K context with LazyMCP. ## How It Works The new endpoint is: ```text /lazymcp ``` There are also scoped variants: ```text /lazymcp/{server_or_group} /toolset/{toolset_name}/lazymcp ``` The basic flow is: ### 1. Check Status Call `mcp_status` with: ```json {} ``` It returns whether LazyMCP is enabled, how many servers are visible, and how many tools are available behind the gateway. ### 2. Discover Servers Call `mcp_describe` with: ```json {} ``` This returns a compact catalog of visible servers. In many cases the agent does not need to call this first, because the LazyMCP tool description already includes a one-line summary per visible MCP server using the description configured in LiteLLM. ### 3. Discover One Server Call `mcp_describe` with: ```json {"server":"memory"} ``` This returns the tools available for that server. ### 4. Inspect One Tool Schema Call `mcp_describe` with: ```json {"server":"memory","tool":"memory-find"} ``` At this point the full input schema appears, but only for that specific tool. ### 5. Execute Call `mcp_call` with: ```json { "server": "memory", "tool": "memory-find", "arguments": { "query": "LiteLLM LazyMCP PR status" } } ``` The execution still goes through the real MCP system. ## Security and Compatibility LazyMCP is not a backdoor and does not bypass MCP access control. The implementation preserves the existing controls: - API key permissions, - team permissions, - toolsets, - access groups, - OAuth headers, - dynamic per-server headers, - disabled tools, - IP filters, - live permission re-checks before describe and call. This matters because the LazyMCP catalog can be cached briefly to reduce overhead. Even then, before returning sensitive metadata or executing a tool, LiteLLM re-checks which servers and tools are visible for the current request. In the Responses API path, a verified client IP is propagated through the LazyMCP flow. If no verified IP is available, LazyMCP uses a fail-closed sentinel so IP-restricted servers do not appear by accident. For standard MCP in Responses, the previous behavior is preserved for backward compatibility. ## Why This Matters for Agents Modern coding agents do not just need tool calls. They need context for: - user instructions, - files, - diffs, - errors, - logs, - test results, - outputs from other systems, - previous decisions. Every token spent describing an irrelevant tool is a token that cannot be used to understand the task. LazyMCP makes the initial context more like an index than a full encyclopedia. The agent knows how to ask, but it does not load all content until it needs it. ## Dashboard Change The LiteLLM dashboard adds a `LazyMCP Connect` tab next to the existing MCP connection flow. The tab helps users copy the correct URL for compatible clients: ```text https:///lazymcp ``` or for a toolset: ```text https:///toolset//lazymcp ``` This avoids having to remember the routes manually. ## Type ✅ New Feature ✅ Performance Improvements ✅ UI/UX Improvement ## Changes - Adds `/lazymcp`, `/lazymcp/{server_or_group}`, and `/toolset/{toolset_name}/lazymcp` endpoints backed by a compact LazyMCP gateway exposing only `mcp_describe`, `mcp_call`, and `mcp_status`. - Preserves existing MCP access controls: permissions, access groups, toolsets, OAuth headers, dynamic auth headers, disabled tools, IP filtering, and live permission re-checks for calls/descriptions. - Integrates LazyMCP into Responses/Chat MCP flows while keeping standard Responses MCP backward-compatible when no verified client IP is available. - Adds a LazyMCP Connect tab in the MCP dashboard UI. - Adds focused regression coverage for LazyMCP routing, catalog/cache behavior, toolset authorization, IP filtering, stale-cache denial, Responses auto-execution, and UI tab rendering. ## Testing - `uv run black litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/mcp_server_manager.py litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/server.py litellm/proxy/litellm_pre_call_utils.py litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py litellm/responses/main.py litellm/responses/mcp/chat_completions_handler.py litellm/responses/mcp/litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py litellm/responses/mcp/mcp_streaming_iterator.py litellm/responses/utils.py litellm/types/proxy/litellm_pre_call_utils.py tests/test_litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/test_mcp_server.py tests/test_litellm/responses/mcp/test_litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py` - `uv run ruff check litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/mcp_server_manager.py litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/server.py litellm/proxy/litellm_pre_call_utils.py litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py litellm/responses/main.py litellm/responses/mcp/chat_completions_handler.py litellm/responses/mcp/litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py litellm/responses/mcp/mcp_streaming_iterator.py litellm/responses/utils.py litellm/types/proxy/litellm_pre_call_utils.py tests/test_litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/test_mcp_server.py tests/test_litellm/responses/mcp/test_litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py` - `uv run mypy litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/server.py litellm/responses/mcp/litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py litellm/responses/main.py litellm/responses/mcp/chat_completions_handler.py` - `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/responses/mcp/test_litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py -q` -> 34 passed - `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/test_mcp_server.py -k 'lazymcp or toolset_cache or verified_mcp_client_ip' -q` -> 29 passed, 53 deselected - `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/responses/mcp/test_litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py tests/test_litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/test_mcp_server.py --cov=litellm --cov-report=xml --cov-report=term && uv run diff-cover coverage.xml --compare-branch=origin/litellm_oss_staging --fail-under=0` -> 83% diff coverage locally ## Notes This is a clean branch rebuilt from `origin/litellm_oss_staging`. It replaces PR #27754, which was closed to remove the noisy review history after incorporating review feedback. @greptileai please review.

The agent needs context to read code, understand instructions, inspect diffs, review errors, and reason about the task. If a large part of the context is occupied by irrelevant tool schemas, the model works with more noise and less useful space. ## The LazyMCP Idea LazyMCP changes when tool information is delivered. With direct MCP: ```text Agent -> receives all tools and all schemas -> decides what to use ``` With LazyMCP: ```text Agent -> receives 3 meta-tools -> discovers what it needs -> executes what it needs ``` The agent starts with a minimal interface: ```text mcp_status mcp_describe mcp_call ``` Then it can ask: ```json {"server":"memory"} ``` or even: ```json {"server":"memory","tool":"memory-find"} ``` Only then does it receive the input schema for the tool it needs. ## Comparison in OpenCode The best way to explain this is visually. ### Direct MCP The agent sees a large tool list from the first turn. Many tools may be unrelated to the current task. Conceptual example: ```text memory-find memory-store github-list-issues github-create-pr browser-navigate browser-click qdrant-search calendar-create-event drive-search ... ``` Each tool brings its schema. The cost is paid every time, even if the agent only uses one tool. Example of a simple request using 96K out of 262K context because direct MCP loads the full tool catalog up front. ### LazyMCP The agent sees this: ```text mcp_status mcp_describe mcp_call ``` When it needs memory, it asks about memory. When it needs GitHub, it asks about GitHub. When it needs to execute a tool, it calls `mcp_call`. This reduces initial context and helps the model focus on the task. Example of the same simple request using 24K out of 262K context with LazyMCP. ## How It Works The new endpoint is: ```text /lazymcp ``` There are also scoped variants: ```text /lazymcp/{server_or_group} /toolset/{toolset_name}/lazymcp ``` The basic flow is: ### 1. Check Status Call `mcp_status` with: ```json {} ``` It returns whether LazyMCP is enabled, how many servers are visible, and how many tools are available behind the gateway. ### 2. Discover Servers Call `mcp_describe` with: ```json {} ``` This returns a compact catalog of visible servers. In many cases the agent does not need to call this first, because the LazyMCP tool description already includes a one-line summary per visible MCP server using the description configured in LiteLLM. ### 3. Discover One Server Call `mcp_describe` with: ```json {"server":"memory"} ``` This returns the tools available for that server. ### 4. Inspect One Tool Schema Call `mcp_describe` with: ```json {"server":"memory","tool":"memory-find"} ``` At this point the full input schema appears, but only for that specific tool. ### 5. Execute Call `mcp_call` with: ```json { "server": "memory", "tool": "memory-find", "arguments": { "query": "LiteLLM LazyMCP PR status" } } ``` The execution still goes through the real MCP system. ## Security and Compatibility LazyMCP is not a backdoor and does not bypass MCP access control. The implementation preserves the existing controls: - API key permissions, - team permissions, - toolsets, - access groups, - OAuth headers, - dynamic per-server headers, - disabled tools, - IP filters, - live permission re-checks before describe and call. This matters because the LazyMCP catalog can be cached briefly to reduce overhead. Even then, before returning sensitive metadata or executing a tool, LiteLLM re-checks which servers and tools are visible for the current request. In the Responses API path, a verified client IP is propagated through the LazyMCP flow. If no verified IP is available, LazyMCP uses a fail-closed sentinel so IP-restricted servers do not appear by accident. For standard MCP in Responses, the previous behavior is preserved for backward compatibility. ## Why This Matters for Agents Modern coding agents do not just need tool calls. They need context for: - user instructions, - files, - diffs, - errors, - logs, - test results, - outputs from other systems, - previous decisions. Every token spent describing an irrelevant tool is a token that cannot be used to understand the task. LazyMCP makes the initial context more like an index than a full encyclopedia. The agent knows how to ask, but it does not load all content until it needs it. ## Dashboard Change The LiteLLM dashboard adds a `LazyMCP Connect` tab next to the existing MCP connection flow. The tab helps users copy the correct URL for compatible clients: ```text https:///lazymcp ``` or for a toolset: ```text https:///toolset//lazymcp ``` This avoids having to remember the routes manually. ## Type ✅ New Feature ✅ Performance Improvements ✅ UI/UX Improvement ## Changes - Adds `/lazymcp`, `/lazymcp/{server_or_group}`, and `/toolset/{toolset_name}/lazymcp` endpoints backed by a compact LazyMCP gateway exposing only `mcp_describe`, `mcp_call`, and `mcp_status`. - Preserves existing MCP access controls: permissions, access groups, toolsets, OAuth headers, dynamic auth headers, disabled tools, IP filtering, and live permission re-checks for calls/descriptions. - Integrates LazyMCP into Responses/Chat MCP flows while keeping standard Responses MCP backward-compatible when no verified client IP is available. - Adds a LazyMCP Connect tab in the MCP dashboard UI. - Adds focused regression coverage for LazyMCP routing, catalog/cache behavior, toolset authorization, IP filtering, stale-cache denial, Responses auto-execution, and UI tab rendering. ## Testing - `uv run black litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/mcp_server_manager.py litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/server.py litellm/proxy/litellm_pre_call_utils.py litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py litellm/responses/main.py litellm/responses/mcp/chat_completions_handler.py litellm/responses/mcp/litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py litellm/responses/mcp/mcp_streaming_iterator.py litellm/responses/utils.py litellm/types/proxy/litellm_pre_call_utils.py tests/test_litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/test_mcp_server.py tests/test_litellm/responses/mcp/test_litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py` - `uv run ruff check litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/mcp_server_manager.py litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/server.py litellm/proxy/litellm_pre_call_utils.py litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py litellm/responses/main.py litellm/responses/mcp/chat_completions_handler.py litellm/responses/mcp/litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py litellm/responses/mcp/mcp_streaming_iterator.py litellm/responses/utils.py litellm/types/proxy/litellm_pre_call_utils.py tests/test_litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/test_mcp_server.py tests/test_litellm/responses/mcp/test_litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py` - `uv run mypy litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/server.py litellm/responses/mcp/litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py litellm/responses/main.py litellm/responses/mcp/chat_completions_handler.py` - `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/responses/mcp/test_litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py -q` -> 34 passed - signal.title: fix(ui): render the correct widget for nullable MCP tool schema properties
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Optional MCP tool parameters get no input field in the Tool Testing Playground - The same nullable fields submit with the wrong value type in the chat playground How it solves it: - Resolve JSON Schema's array `type` (e.g. `["string", "null"]`) to its real type - Use that resolved type everywhere a widget or a value conversion depends on it ## User Flow Before: an admin testing an MCP tool with optional parameters in the Tool Testing Playground cannot fill in those parameters at all 1. They open the MCP Servers page, pick a connected server, and open the Tool Testing Playground for a tool with optional parameters (for example an Azure DevOps MCP server's `testplan_test_suite_write`, whose `parentSuiteId` and `name` are optional) 2. Required parameters show a labeled input, but each optional parameter shows only its label and an info icon, with no field to type into 3. They cannot exercise the tool's optional parameters at all After: the same optional parameters show a usable input matching their real type 1. They open the same Tool Testing Playground for the same tool 2. Optional parameters now show the right input for their type: a number field for `parentSuiteId`, a text field for `name` 3. They fill in a value and click Call Tool, and the request carries that value with the correct type ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review Verified locally: `npx vitest run` on both touched test files (8/8 passing), `npx eslint` on all five changed files (0 errors; warning counts identical before/after, confirmed by diffing against each file's pre-fix version), `npx prettier --check` (clean), and a full-project `npx tsc --noEmit` (0 errors touching any of the changed files; the errors it does report are pre-existing and unrelated, in files this PR does not touch). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix No live proxy/browser screenshot here since this fix has no backend surface to curl; the reported bug and the fix are both purely in how the dashboard renders an MCP tool's JSON Schema. Proof instead is a real, mutation-sensitive test run: the same two new tests run against the code before and after the fix, showing they fail on the reported bug and pass once it is fixed. **Before (parent commit `423b791ee0395815050998dd73542445350ab792`): the reported bug, reproduced** ``` $ git stash push -- ui/litellm-dashboard/src/app/\(dashboard\)/mcp-servers/_components/ToolTestPanel.tsx ui/litellm-dashboard/src/components/mcp_tools/types.tsx $ npx vitest run "src/app/(dashboard)/mcp-servers/_components/ToolTestPanel.test.tsx" ❯ ToolTestPanel defaults > renders inputs for nullable (type-array) schema properties instead of leaving them blank → Unable to find a label with the text of: parentSuiteId Test Files 1 failed (1) Tests 2 failed | 4 passed (6) ``` The failure is exactly the reported symptom: a schema property typed `["integer", "null"]` (JSON Schema's nullable-field shape, the one Pydantic's `model_json_schema()` emits for `Optional[int]`) gets no associated form control at all, so `getByLabelText` cannot find one. **After (this PR, commit `2fd574308e...`): same test, same schema, fixed** ``` $ git stash pop $ npx vitest run "src/app/(dashboard)/mcp-servers/_components/ToolTestPanel.test.tsx" "src/components/mcp_tools/MCPToolArgumentsForm.test.tsx" ✓ src/app/(dashboard)/mcp-servers/_components/ToolTestPanel.test.tsx (6 tests) ✓ src/components/mcp_tools/MCPToolArgumentsForm.test.tsx (2 tests) Test Files 2 passed (2) Tests 8 passed (8) ``` `MCPToolArgumentsForm` (the chat playground's tool-argument form, which shares the identical schema-typing bug behind a different symptom: it has a fallback branch, so a nullable integer field rendered as a plain text input instead of vanishing) is fixed by the same change and covered by its own new test file, since it had none before. ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ✅ Test ## Caveats (if any) - No screenshot/live-proxy proof; this bug and fix are both pure frontend schema-rendering, nothing to curl - Fixes two components (`ToolTestPanel`, `MCPToolArgumentsForm`) since both duplicate the same schema-parsing logic and share the identical root cause; not splitting into two PRs since neither fix is meaningful alone against the shared `InputSchemaProperty.type` contract this PR also widens ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: feat(gemini): allow disabling thought summaries while keeping thinking on
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - both reasoning-effort mappers hardcode `includeThoughts: True` whenever thinking is on, so thinking ON with summaries OFF is unreachable, even though that is the default of Google's own SDK - for callers who discard the summaries, they are pure added latency: the model reasons the same either way, the response just carries the narration back How it solves it: - adds `litellm.gemini_include_thoughts_default`, defaulting to `True` so nothing changes for anyone who does not set it ## User Flow An operator fronting Vertex Gemini sets `litellm.gemini_include_thoughts_default = False` once at gateway startup. Requests then go out with `thinkingLevel`/`thinkingBudget` intact and no `includeThoughts`, matching what a direct google SDK call sends. Reasoning is unchanged, the summary text is not returned Leaving it alone sends exactly what LiteLLM sends today ## Relevant issues Closes #36401 ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix I went with option 2 from the issue, the module flag, rather than option 1, the request param. It mirrors `litellm.enable_gemini_default_thinking_level_low` which already lives in this same file for the same kind of decision, and it needs no `supported_openai_params` plumbing or per-provider passthrough. The reported use case is a gateway-wide latency choice, which a module flag covers. Happy to add the request param on top if you would rather have per-request control ```bash $ python -c " import litellm from litellm.llms.vertex_ai.gemini.vertex_and_google_ai_studio_gemini import VertexGeminiConfig as C print('default ', C._map_reasoning_effort_to_thinking_level('medium', model='gemini-3-pro-preview')) litellm.gemini_include_thoughts_default = False print('summaries off', C._map_reasoning_effort_to_thinking_level('medium', model='gemini-3-pro-preview')) print('disable ', C._map_reasoning_effort_to_thinking_level('disable', model='gemini-3-pro-preview'))" default {'thinkingLevel': 'high', 'includeThoughts': True} summaries off {'thinkingLevel': 'high', 'includeThoughts': False} disable {'thinkingLevel': 'low', 'includeThoughts': False} ``` The whole gemini suite still passes: ```bash $ pytest tests/test_litellm/llms/vertex_ai/gemini/ -q 278 passed, 1 skipped ``` ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats (if any) The flag gates three call sites, not two: the `thinkingBudget` mapper, the `thinkingLevel` mapper, and `_map_thinking_param`, which handles the anthropic-style `thinking={"type": "enabled"}` shape. All three answer the same question, so leaving the third one hardcoded would have made the flag behave differently depending on which parameter spelling the caller reached for The `disable` and `none` paths still force `includeThoughts: False` regardless of the flag. With thinking off there is nothing to summarise, and the flag is about reachability rather than forcing summaries on ## QA runbook Point the proxy at Vertex Gemini, send a request with `reasoning_effort: "medium"` and `--detailed_debug`, and confirm the outbound `thinkingConfig` carries `includeThoughts: true`. Set `litellm.gemini_include_thoughts_default = False`, restart, resend, and confirm it is `false` while `thinkingLevel` is unchanged and `reasoning_tokens` in the response stays in the same range ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: feat: add FlexAI as an OpenAI-compatible provider
signal.text: ## Relevant issues New provider registration (no linked issue). Follows [Adding OpenAI-Compatible Providers](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/contributing/adding_openai_compatible_providers) and `litellm/llms/openai_like/README.md`. ## What this adds [FlexAI](https://flex.ai)'s Token Service is an OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint (`https://api.flex.ai/v1`) serving open-weight models — Qwen3.x, DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.2, gpt-oss, Llama 3.x, Gemma 4, Mistral — plus embedding, image, and speech models. | File | Change | | --- | --- | | `litellm/llms/openai_like/providers.json` | `flexai` entry: `base_url=https://api.flex.ai/v1`, `FLEXAI_API_KEY`, `FLEXAI_API_BASE` override, `base_class=openai_gpt`, `/v1/chat/completions` + `/v1/responses` | | `litellm/constants.py` | `flexai` in `openai_compatible_providers`; `https://api.flex.ai/v1` in `openai_compatible_endpoints` | | `litellm/litellm_core_utils/get_llm_provider_logic.py` | base-URL autodetection — `api_base=https://api.flex.ai/v1` resolves to `flexai`, preferring an explicit `api_key` over the server environment | | `litellm/types/utils.py` | `FLEXAI` in the `LlmProviders` enum | | `model_prices_and_context_window.json` | 21 entries for the served roster | | `litellm/model_prices_and_context_window_backup.json` | same 21 entries (asserted byte-identical by a test — see note below) | | `provider_endpoints_support.json` | endpoint-support block | | `tests/test_litellm/llms/openai_like/test_flexai_provider.py` | 18 tests | No `param_mappings` needed — verified `max_completion_tokens` is accepted natively. ```python import litellm response = litellm.completion( model="flexai/gpt-oss-120b", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}], ) ``` ## How the pricing entries were produced Generated from FlexAI's **public** model feed — `https://tokens.flex.ai/api/models` (no key required, curl-able by a reviewer) — and then cross-checked field-by-field against authenticated prod `GET /v1/models`. Every entry carries a `source` pointing at that feed. Roster and price agreement, verified **2026-08-04** (FlexAI's served set changes as models are pinned/unpinned, so treat the feed above as the source of truth rather than this snapshot): ``` prod /v1/models : 21 models committed flexai/* : 21 entries in prod, NOT committed : none committed, NOT in prod : none price spot-check (prod pricing.prompt vs committed input_cost_per_token): bge-m3 prod=1e-08 committed=1e-08 MATCH DeepSeek-V4-Flash prod=8.96e-08 committed=8.96e-08 MATCH gemma-4-26B-A4B-it prod=6e-08 committed=6e-08 MATCH GLM-4.5-Air-FP8 prod=1.25e-07 committed=1.25e-07 MATCH GLM-5.2 prod=4.018e-07 committed=4.018e-07 MATCH gpt-oss-120b prod=3.9e-08 committed=3.9e-08 MATCH ``` Both cost-map files were edited by **text splice** rather than a `json.dump` rewrite, so every other entry is byte-identical — the diff is 255 pure insertions per file, zero deletions. Validated against `model_prices_and_context_window.schema.json` (0 errors). ## Live verification from this branch Against prod `https://api.flex.ai/v1`: ``` completion() -> HTTP 200 model=flexai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash tokens=11/2 cost=$0.0000013440 (= 11 x 8.96e-08 + 2 x 1.792e-07, so the cost-map lookup resolves) max_completion_tokens accepted -> yes (no param_mappings needed) responses() -> HTTP 200 ``` ## Checks run - `pytest tests/test_litellm/llms/openai_like/test_flexai_provider.py -q` → **18 passed** - `pytest tests/test_litellm/llms/openai_like/ tests/litellm/llms/openai_like/ -q` → **148 passed, 5 skipped** - `python tests/code_coverage_tests/check_provider_folders_documented.py` → passes (`All 27 openai_like providers are documented`) - `python tests/code_coverage_tests/check_get_model_cost_key_performance.py` → passes - `jsonschema` validation of the new entries against `model_prices_and_context_window.schema.json` → 0 errors - `ruff check` on each changed source file → finding count unchanged vs `HEAD` (`constants.py` 201→201, `get_llm_provider_logic.py` 15→15); the new test file has the same 4 findings as the existing `test_pinstripes_provider.py` baseline, and `ruff.toml` excludes `tests/*` from lint ## Two notes for the reviewer **1. The packaged backup copy.** `litellm/model_prices_and_context_window_backup.json` is what `GetModelCostMap.load_local_model_cost_map()` reads, so a provider whose entries land only in the root file gets `"This model isn't mapped yet"` whenever the remote map is unavailable or `LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True`. I hit exactly that, so both files are updated, and `test_flexai_entries_match_packaged_backup` asserts they stay in sync. Happy to drop that test if the backup is meant to be regenerated by tooling instead. **2. Non-chat models are priced but not yet routable.** 5 of the 21 entries are `embedding` / `image_generation` / `audio_transcription` / `audio_speech` for models FlexAI serves. JSON-configured providers currently route only chat completions (`JSONProviderRegistry.exists()` is consulted in `completion()`) and the Responses API, so `provider_endpoints_support.json` honestly declares those endpoints `false`. Their *pricing* is nonetheless correct and calculator-verified — per Greptile's catch, they use the fields the generic calculators actually read (`input_cost_per_image`, `input_cost_per_character`), with tests exercising both calculators. Glad to trim them to chat-only if you'd rather the cost map track routable endpoints exactly. ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests — 18 unit tests, all passing - [x] My PR passes all unit tests on the touched paths (`148 passed, 5 skipped` across both `openai_like` test dirs) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] Bot reviews addressed — Greptile's P2 (non-chat pricing fields) and veria-ai's credential-precedence finding are both fixed, each with regression tests 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_013jmFw7fcJTtdTgmkKJa5yr

signal.title: [Bug]: LiteLLM_VerificationToken.spend remains 0 while SpendLogs accumulates spend
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? # Bug: LiteLLM_VerificationToken.spend remains 0 while SpendLogs accumulates spend ## Summary We've identified an inconsistency between `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` and `LiteLLM_VerificationToken`. For at least one API key, LiteLLM successfully: - accepts requests - records token usage - calculates request cost - writes non-zero spend into `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` However, the corresponding record in `LiteLLM_VerificationToken` still shows: ```text spend = 0 ``` This causes the UI to display zero spend for the key even though billable traffic exists. --- ## Environment - LiteLLM Proxy - PostgreSQL backend - Model: `<MODEL_NAME>` --- ### User Flow ## Evidence ### VerificationToken record ```sql SELECT key_alias, spend, team_id, max_budget FROM "LiteLLM_VerificationToken" WHERE token='<API_KEY_1>';
